speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO THE DEFENDERS OF DIEN BIEN PHU
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps you would allow me to inform the house at this time that on Saturday our ambassador in Paris was asked to convey a message to Prime Minister Laniel of France, on behalf of the Prime Minister and government of Canada, to express to the French government and people the sincere and heartfelt tribute of Canadians for the matchless heroism of the soldiers of France and Viet Nam. With all free men, Canadians, while lamenting the tragic ending of the legendary conflict at Dien Bien Phu, salute with pride and honour the heroic defenders of the fortress. Hon. members will note that this message is very similar in content to the message released Friday evening by the Secretary of State for External Affairs at Geneva, of which he gave a copy to the French delegation there.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TRIBUTE TO THE DEFENDERS OF DIEN BIEN PHU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members will wish to express their approval of the message which has been sent and to join in the sentiments of admiration for those who have died in the cause of freedom. Without in any way referring to the military conditions, there is not one of us who can fail to have been deeply moved by the thought that others have been dying in these past few days fighting against that evil force to which all of us are so strongly opposed. Whatever the outcome of this struggle may be, their sacrifice will not have been in vain if what has happened at Dien Bien Phu serves to bring home to the free world a full realization of the nature of the evil against which we are at this time building up our strength. Let us hope there will be peace; but it will only come if we recognize the reality of the things to which we are opposed.
As we pay tribute to the men who died I think all of us should also pay attention to an incident that happened in the French chamber of deputies last Friday. If anyone ever had any doubt where the loyalty of communists in any country lies, it was clarified on the floor of the French Chamber of Deputies when Premier Laniel asked the
deputies to rise in tribute to the dead at Dien Bien Phu. When the communist members refused to rise, disloyalty in all its naked ugliness was then disclosed. There was a symbol for the whole world of what the communist in every free land really is. He expresses loyalty to no flag, to no faith, to no country. There is no loyalty except to the Kremlin itself. We should bow our heads for those who died and carry in our hearts the warning that came to us from Paris on Friday.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: That a special committee consisting of 31 members, to be designated by the house at a later date, be appointed to consider the bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and the bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces, and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee; that the said committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records, to print from day to day its minutes of proceedings and evidence, to sit while the house is sitting and to report from time to time; that the quorum of the said committee shall consist of ten members; and that the provisions of standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
Is the minister going to make a statement on the resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
It is not my intention to make any lengthy statement at this time. In the past I have expressed the government's policy, as my predecessors have done, that whenever any important or major changes in veterans legislation were introduced, a special committee on veterans affairs would be set up in order that these major changes might be given more detailed study in this committee. I believe the last committee was established in 1952.
This year the government has put forward substantial changes in veterans legislation, and for this reason we have thought it advisable the special committee should be
Committee on Veterans Affairs set up. As hon. members know, some of this legislation has already been introduced in this house, and has been referred to the committee we are about to set up. I am referring to the War Service Grants Act, and the bill concerning benefits for members of the Canadian forces. These two pieces of legislation were introduced in order to put into statutory form the benefits given to members of our armed forces who had seen service in Korea, and make those benefits parallel to those given men who served in world war II.
One other piece of legislation has been introduced and has already been passed by this house without reference to this committee. I refer to the educational assistance bill. At that time it was not thought necessary to send this measure to the committee, because only minor adjustments were made and the need for them had only become apparent after the legislation had been in force for a period of one year. There is on the order paper now a bill to amend the Pension Act. It is my intention at a very early date to introduce further legislation to amend the Veterans Land Act, bringing about some major changes in that act.

I wish to thank the minister, Mr. Speaker, for his explanation of the resolution. I believe everyone is familiar with this resolution. If they are not, there is no reason why they should not be, because I do not know of any resolution that has been on the order paper for such a long time as this one to set up a veterans committee. We asked for a veterans committee when we came to this session of parliament last November. Resolutions and bills have come and gone; but this resolution which was put on the order paper over three months ago is just being passed today. I am sure if the minister has used the word "stand" once in connection with it, he has used that word at least thirty or forty times. There is no doubt he has established a long-distance record, so far as the resolution is concerned.
However, we are pleased today to find that at last it has been moved, and we hope that it will be passed-indeed we know it will be-so that a veterans committee will be set up. It is hard for many of us to understand why it has taken so long to bring the resolution before the house. We are now approaching, we hope, a time near the end of the session, a time when all members are crowded with work both in the committees and in the house. The estimates are now being considered. There are many important matters mentioned in those estimates, and most members like to attend while they are under
4552	HOUSE OF
Committee on Veterans Affairs consideration in order either to criticize or to get information concerning estimates affecting their own constituencies.
Also we hear at this time rumours about morning sittings. As I say, at this crowded period of the session we have placed before us this resolution to set up a committee which, to my mind, should have been set up many months ago. I have heard no explanation from the minister as to why he has waited so long. My own opinion is that the government has not been able to agree on the legislation to be brought before the committee on veterans affairs.
To my mind the most important legislation with which we will have to deal at this session will be that referring to the veterans. I say that legislation of other departments should not have preference over that dealing with this very important subject.
What I have said serves as a further argument for what we have sought on many occasions, namely the setting up of a permanent veterans affairs committee. Time and again we have pointed out the great advantages there would be in having such a committee. We have also pointed out that since 1916, when the first veterans committee was appointed in the House of Commons, some twenty committees have been set up. This in itself I suggest is an indication that this is a permanent matter, and that there is a necessity for setting up a permanent committee to attend to veterans affairs.
Before the second great war we had before us only those matters dealing with the veterans of the first great war. Today however the situation is entirely different. Not only must we consider the problems of veterans of the first war, but we have also those of the second war. Added to this we must consider the problems of veterans of the Korean war, the men who are serving in Europe, and the men in the reserve army. All these subjects are included in veterans affairs. Today the problems of those who served in the first war are entirely different from those who served in the second war. We know that veterans of the first war have today reached the age of sixty or seventy. So far as they are concerned, their particular interest is that having to do with pensions, hospitalization, war veterans allowances, old soldiers homes and other subjects along those lines.
We know that men who served in the second world war have been established in different professions, and that their problems are quite different. Again, the problems of the young men who have served in Korea are different. Briefly, it will be a long time, Mr. Speaker-it may not be in our time, or even


in our children's time-before the House of Commons will not be dealing with veterans problems.
For these reasons I say a permanent veterans committee should be set up to deal with matters of this kind. In the past we have criticized the size of the veterans committee. Perhaps no great argument could be advanced against the committee of thirty-one members now suggested, other than the fact that it is not broad enough to include a large number of members in the House of Commons who wish to serve on it. During the term of the last parliament I believe there were eighty veterans who were members of the House of Commons. While I have not made a count of the veterans in this parliament, I understand there are more than in the last one. I know many of these members are disappointed that they are not permitted to serve on this committee. For instance, the party to which I belong is allowed only six members. Yet, in it there are twice that many who would like to serve on this committee. And I believe the same could be said of the other parties in the house.
There is a good precedent for establishing large veterans committees. I recall that when we were studying a veterans charter after the second world war the late Ian Mackenzie, who was then minister of veterans affairs, wanted a large committee. The result was that in 1945 a committee of sixty members was established, and again in 1946 a committee having the same number of members. But in 1948 the number was reduced to thirty-five, and in the last few years it has gone down to thirty-one. I would like to see the present committee a larger and perhaps a more representative one.
I now come to the object of setting up veterans committees. As I said a moment ago, we must deal with the problems of veterans who have served in different wars-and when I referred to the matter earlier I might also have mentioned the veterans of the South African war and those of the Riel rebellion. The object of setting up the committee should be that of dealing with the many problems these veterans must face. After the second world war the veterans committee met for many weeks with the result that we produced what has come to be known as the veterans charter. Members of that committee, and of the committee in parliament in general, have been proud to call that charter one of the most up-to-date pieces of legislation to be found anywhere. But there are weaknesses in all legislation, and, as time

has proven since 1945 and 1946, many amendments have had to be made to this legislation to meet changing conditions and circumstances. Today when a committee is set up it is set up not to consider what we think are all the problems concerning veterans but those few problems which the government itself feels should come before it.
The most important part of the resolution which is now before us is, of course, our terms of reference. Again we have the same criticism to make of the terms of reference setting up this committee as we have had of the terms of reference setting up committees in the past. It should be the duty of a veterans affairs committee to investigate each and every problem which concerns veterans.
We have been told by the minister this afternoon-and it is mentioned in the resolution-the matters which we shall be allowed to consider. We know that we shall be permitted to deal with and consider Bill No. 82, as he mentioned. In his remarks the minister stated that the government sets up these committees when there are major changes to be considered in the act. Well, as far as Bill No. 82 is concerned, no great major changes are being made in the War Service Grants Act. The bill has had second reading. It has been before this house, and I do not think that veterans across the country believe that any great major changes are being made in the act.
It was found that certain veterans had not taken their re-establishment credit; others had not applied for their gratuities. It is a matter of routine, Mr. Speaker, that is being dealt with in Bill No. 82. We are asked to extend the time so that these returned soldiers may make application for re-establishment credit and for their gratuities.
Bill No. 101 is another piece of legislation that is being sent to this committee. Is there any hon. member who will say that there is anything urgent contained in Bill No. 101; that there are any great major changes such as the minister would lead us to believe the government felt was necessary as far as Bill No. 101 was concerned? It simply extends the benefits received by veterans during world war II to the men who fought in Korea. It is an obvious thing; it is routine. We have been extending benefits for the last three or four years.
We now come to Bill No. 339, which was mentioned by the minister this afternoon. Perhaps there is more reason for the Pension Act to be sent to this committee than there is for those others which I have mentioned.
Committee on Veterans Affairs But no great changes are being made in the Pension Act. When it comes before the committee the minister will find out that more changes are left out of the bill which should be considered than are contained in the bill. The only great change that I see is that referring to benefits for adopted children. It affects very few. Then again, it takes away from parliament the right to set the salaries of the commissioners and places it in the hands of the governor in council. I ask you, Mr. Speaker; is there any great demand in this house or across the country, and more particularly by veterans of this country, for this particular legislation? These are the great major changes that the government wants us to deal with. I assure them that these are changes that do not affect to any great extent the veterans of this country.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that the Veterans Land Act would be amended. We have had rumours to that effect. It has been asked for by veterans. Legislation will have to do with housing, which is one of the great problems not only of veterans but of all people in Canada. We are pleased that there will be amendments to this act. We hope that the amendments will be such that they will be of great benefit to the veterans. But here again, if the rumours I hear are true, it is not going to involve any great financial outlay as far as this government is concerned.
My understanding of the amendments to the Veterans Land Act is that they are going to decrease the amount of land which is necessary upon which a veteran may wish to build a house; they are going to make arrangements so that it will be easier for him to borrow money. But it is to be a revolving fund that the veteran will have to pay back. The veteran will have to pay back to the government the money which is borrowed for the building of his own house. No, Mr. Speaker, I contend that in setting up this committee the government should have made the terms of reference wide enough to deal with veterans affairs. We should not be told that these are the only matters to which we can give consideration, because there is no body of men in Canada better qualified to judge the problems of veterans than the veterans themselves, veterans who are members of the House of Commons, and the veterans organizations across Canada who would appear before this committee to point out some of the great weaknesses in the act and some of the requirements of veterans.
This committee is to be given absolutely no initiative. We are simply told that this

Committee on Veterans Off airs is the legislation that we shall have to deal with and that is all we can deal with. As I said a moment ago, we know of the existing problems but our hands are tied as far as being able to deal with those problems is concerned.
I now come to what I consider to be the outstanding problem of veterans in Canada today. It is not those amendments to the War Service Grants Act; it is not those amendments to Bill No. 101; it is not Bill No. 339. To a certain extent it is the Veterans Land Act, because, as I said a moment ago, it deals with housing. That is one of the great problems; but the great problem which is on the tongue of practically every veteran in Canada today is: What is this government going to do regarding war veterans allowances? That is the problem that should be before parliament and this veterans affairs committee. It is the one that should have been given first consideration. It is the one which receives the first recommendation from every veterans organization in Canada, whether it be the Canadian Legion, National Council of Veterans, the Amputations Association or any other organized veterans association in this country. It is also one which, as I said a moment ago, the individual veteran across this country feels should have first consideration. In the past when veterans affairs were being considered, especially when the war veterans allowance was under consideration, I have taken the time, as have other hon. members, to set out the history of war veterans allowances. The pages of Hansard contain the details of that history and I am not going to take the time of the house this afternoon to review it because I do not feel it is necessary. I believe the history of the war veterans allowance is well known to every hon. member in this house. That legislation is recognized and has been for some time as one of the great steps forward in veterans legislation, and I might add that it has been and is a great blessing to thousands of veterans all across this country as well as to their dependents.
Hon. members will recall that legislation was passed in 1930 and at first the amount was $20 per month. It was raised to $40 per month, which was the basic rate, and it is now $50 per month. That is the amount the single veteran receives in war veterans allowance, and the married veteran and his wife receive a total of $90 per month. Possibly we might ask ourselves why this legislation should be considered at this time. Well, there are many strong arguments and they have all been presented to the government. Old soldiers, now in their late sixties and many of them now seventy, have no other income but $50 per month. With the high cost of


rent and the high cost of everything which goes to make the cost of living, he is finding it very difficult to exist, and many of them are living below subsistence level. There are other old soldiers with small disability pensions which are augmented by the war veterans allowance, but they are not allowed to receive the full amount of war veterans allowance because of the ceiling which has been set on that allowance. I believe the most absurd provision in the war veterans allowance at the present time is this ceiling.

Where the business before the house is a motion to provide machinery, it is not in order to discuss the merits of the policy which it is sought to put into operation. There are other citations, of course, which I could quote at this moment, but whereas it is the sense of the house to have as generous

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member has perhaps indicated more clearly than I did the exact purport of my remarks. Hon. members should not go into details with respect to the two bills which are now being referred to the committee in this resolution. These two amending bills were introduced through the proper channels, namely on resolution, then later first reading and second reading. The principle has been debated and after second reading, in accordance with the provisions of standing order 50, they were referred to a special committee to be

Committee on Veterans Affairs appointed later. Hon. members should not go into the provisions of those two bills. By the same token, while they may argue that the terms of reference should be widened, they should not go into the provisions of the bills which they would like to see covered by the terms of this resolution.
There is, however, one point that I should like the hon. member to examine carefully. Let us examine what is meant by "such other legislation relating to veterans affairs". What is meant by that phrase? It does not mean such other statutes as are now in existence. What is meant by that phrase is such other amending bills as may be introduced in the same manner as that in which were introduced the two bills mentioned in this resolution. They are the ones that are contemplated by those words "such other legislation relating to veterans affairs". If they are introduced by the government, the discussion which is now taking place about them may be completely superfluous. That is a point that I should like the hon. member to consider because, as he knows, if it was existing statutes such as the War Veterans Allowance Act which were contemplated by "such other legislation", the terms of reference would not read as they do now. The terms of reference would be "to consider such appropriate amendments to be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act". What is contemplated by "such other legislation" is a bill. As hon. members know,
The most important functions of a parliamentary body may be stated as-

. . . for these differing powers different forms of procedure were evolved: for the first,-

-the motion; for legislation, the bill: . . ,
Then what is a bill? A definition will be found at page 84 as follows:
A bill is a draft of a legislative proposal which, when it has been passed by both houses and received the Royal Assent, will become an act of parliament or statute. The first division of bills is into public bills and private bills, the former dealing with public general interests and the latter with local personal interests (see chapters VI and IX).
tMr. Speaker.]

In the class of public bills the important distinction for our present purpose is between a government bill and a private member's bill, the former being introduced and piloted through the house by a member of the government and the latter by a private or (more technically) unofficial member.
What is contemplated by "such other legislation" is government bills which may be introduced in the future.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is what we are hoping for.

I know that is what the hon. member is hoping for; but no matter how hard he may be hoping for it, he must not at this moment deprive himself of the pleasure which he may have later either of heralding the decision of the government on a point in which he is interested or of criticizing the government if they have not brought in the legislative measures which he would like them to introduce.
As I said, on this resolution hon. members may discuss the desirability of appointing the committee. They may discuss the opportunity of widening the powers contained therein. However, they must not go into the merits of existing legislation or proposed changes therein and discuss the various provisions which are contained in that legislation. Otherwise there will be no end to the discussion. It will be difficult for the Chair to preserve order in debate. I do not know how many pieces of legislation are contained in the veterans charter, but if I were to say there were 15, I may not be too far wrong. Maybe there are more. That is a considerable number. On a resolution for the appointment of a committee to consider two amending bills with respect to existing legislation, where members would like to see perhaps 15 amending bills referred to the committee, if I allow them not only to say that the committee's powers should be widened but to discuss the various merits of the provisions of each and every one of these bills, I ask hon. members this question: Where do we stand as far as the rules of the house are concerned? I know that we are all greatly interested in having them preserved.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. There is one feature I should like to draw to Your Honour's attention. If a member is to make the argument that a certain act should be considered by this committee, then surely he should be allowed to say why it is essential that that act should be considered by the committee. I submit that that is all that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) was doing. If Your Honour makes a ruling that we cannot say why we believe a particular measure should

be considered this year by the committee, then in effect Your Honour makes it impossible for us to make a reasoned case for the broadening of the reference to the committee. I submit that that is all that the hon. member for Royal is attempting to do.

The hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green), when a point of order was raised on April 4, 1951, made exactly the same argument. I could quote him as reported on page 1625 of Hansard, April 4, 1951, where he says:
... if you should rule this amendment out of order, then for all practical purposes it would be impossible to move an amendment to any notice of motion of this kind; because there could not be a case in which the amendment would be more relevant to the contents of the notice of motion than is this one.
Then he carries on with the same argument as he put forward a moment ago. As I said, I want to be as generous as I can be, but I do not think hon. members would forgive me if I knowingly permitted the rule of relevancy to be violated in flagrant fashion. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I had made the point that I thought the chief problems of the veterans should be the ones to be considered by the veterans affairs committee. That was the basis of my argument. I followed that by pointing out that the terms of reference of the resolution do not permit us to consider what we believe are some of the big problems. I mentioned particularly the War Veterans Allowance Act which I believe is not to be considered. My basis for
Committee on Veterans Affairs so- stating is the information given us here a few days ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he gave the house a list of the legislation that it is intended to bring forward during the balance of this session. The War Veterans Allowance Act was not included. At that time I asked the Prime Minister if it was intended to introduce legislation respecting the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session and he told me that there would be no further legislation other than that which he had mentioned.
It was for that reason that I was arguing today that the War Veterans Allowance Act should be included. I have not undertaken to say what should be contained in any amendments to that legislation. I have studiously stayed away from that. I have not said that the basic rate should be so much or that the ceiling should be raised. These are things which I feel should be considered by a committee. The committee would obtain information on all these points and would make its recommendations to the government as to what amendments should be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I am not going to labour the point any further. There are other arguments I could use but I do not think it is necessary. I will say, though, that when veterans throughout this country learned that a veterans affairs committee was to be set up at this session I received a great many letters and telegrams expressing the satisfaction of the individual soldier or veteran that such a committee was to be established. Almost invariably the fact was mentioned that now there would be a committee to consider the question of the war veterans allowance. I could read many of the letters and telegrams if I cared to do so. I am sure all other members received similar letters and telegrams.
I might also say that since the announcement of the Prime Minister a few days ago, that the war veterans allowance would not be a subject considered by the committee, I have received many letters from veterans expressing bitterness, regret and disappointment that this very important subject is not going to be considered. It is not too late yet. There is still time for the government to reconsider the resolution. Committee on Veterans Affairs government and the house. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green):
That the motion be amended by inserting after the word "consider" in the third line thereof the words "the War Veterans Allowance Act."
The amended motion would then read:
That a special committee consisting of thirty-one members, to be designated by the house at a later date, be appointed to consider the War Veterans Allowance Act, the bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and the bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces, and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee; that the said committee shall have power to send for persons, papers and records, to print from day to day its minutes of proceedings and evidence, to sit while the house is sitting and to report from time to time; that the quorum of the said committee shall consist of ten members; and that the provisions of standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
I commend the resolution as it would be amended to the very careful consideration of the minister and the government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Royal has moved an amendment which is quite similar to that which he moved on an earlier occasion. On an earlier occasion his amendment was in this form, "such as the War Veterans Allowance Act." This time it is more direct in that it is right at the beginning of the motion and would follow along with the other two bills that are to be referred.
Consistently since 1939 at least my predecessors have ruled out of order all amendments designed to give a committee wider powers than those set out in the notice of motion. I refer hon. members to citation 546 of Beauchesne, third edition, and to rulings by Mr. Speaker Casgrain on March 13, 1939, Journals, page 185; and by Mr. Speaker Macdonald on March 16, 1950, Journals, page 121; on April 4, 1951, page 243 of the Journals; on November 2, 1951, Journals, page 67; and on April 29, 1952, Journals, page 240; then again on April 12, 1948, page 344.
Then in Hansard for April 4, 1951, will be found a lengthy discussion having to do with an amendment of this type, and amongst other members taking part in the discussion were the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Melfort, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I believe hon. members will understand that after so many of my predecessors have ruled so many times in the one direction on this matter, I would be establishing quite a departure in procedure if I were to say now that amendments of this kind are to be allowed.
[Mr. Brooks.l

I feel that the rulings I have mentioned are ample evidence of sound parliamentary practice with respect to the setting up of committees, and especially with respect to the notice which has to be given prior to the setting up of the committee. The rule is well established, and is to the effect that no amendments should be made to the motion for the appointment of a committee that would give the committee greater powers than those set out in the notice. The explanation I gave a moment ago as to what was meant by "such other legislation" pertaining to veterans affairs is quite apropos on this occasion because the hon. member is moving that the committee be empowered to consider the War Veterans Allowance Act.
The War Veterans Allowance Act is an existing statute. Perhaps, in the laudable desire to have the matter examined by the committee, hon. members are mistaking what, in my humble view, is the point. As hon. members know, according to our procedure legislation may be introduced by the government or by the opposition. In this instance a piece of legislation has been introduced by the government and has gone through the various stages required. It is only after second reading that such legislation can be referred to the committee of the whole or to a special or standing committee. There is no standing committee to take care of this class of bills, and a special committee has been constituted. "If it is the desire that, instead of referring the matter to a committee of the whole house, it be referred to a select committee or a joint committee of both houses, such a motion is made immediately after the second reading and, if carried, the bill is referred accordingly." This statement is found in May's fifteenth edition, page 478. The bills we are now referring to this committee are two bills that have gone through the preliminary stages and have been given second reading. After second reading, instead of being referred in the normal way to the committee of the whole, it was considered they should be referred to a special committee and that is the committee now being established. What the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) contemplates by his amendment is not the reference of the same class of bill, but the reference of an existing statute. An amendment should read that the committee should consider appropriate amendments to the statute, and not just consider the statute. Before hon. members pass judgment on that matter, they should know exactly what they are being asked to consider with respect to that act. It is for that reason it is so important that notice be given, then no one will be caught by surprise.

This is a right that the minorities in this house are always quick to claim, and they should therefore respect it when it refers to their amendments just as they do when it refers to amendments that the other side tries to introduce and of which they are not completely aware. This requirement of notice is just as old as the origin of parliamentary practice. When there was no printed order paper, the clerk had to read all the motions that had to be presented, and even in those days an oral notice was required. Now that we have, with the advent of modern machinery, a printed order paper, our standing order says that the notice must be printed forty-eight hours before it is called. I feel that the various rulings I have mentioned, plus citation 546, should be sufficient to make hon. members understand what my position is in this respect. I cannot accept the amendment.
Does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) wish to speak?

speechtext: I am not at this moment prepared to condemn entirely the ruling that was made on that particular occasion, because the house was not caught by surprise. Mr. Speaker, I have had an education in procedure this afternoon which is all to the good, but has not changed anything very much. I wish to join with the last hon. member in stating that in my judgment the whole status of the veterans affairs committee has been changed within the last few years. This committee, up until the time of the setting up of the last committee-and I believe that is where it showed up clearly-was always considered non-partisan. It was picked largely from members of the house who were exmembers of the forces. For a good many years politics, so far as veterans problems were concerned, were completely divorced from the question.
That was done, I think, because previously the committee set up had power to amend and to initiate legislation that was in the best interests of veterans generally. But in the committee now to be established, and in the last committee that was set up, no longer

Committee on Veterans Affairs have we had a veterans affairs committee of that kind. Now it is merely a legislation examining committee, and has power only to deal with legislation that has already been adopted by the government and treasury board. Inevitably, in those circumstances, when such matters are brought before the veterans committee the result is to line up along political lines. It is that change in the status of the committee that is responsible. I suggest it is a bad development.
In the last sitting of this committee on veterans affairs-and I am reasonably sure the condition will be the same with this one- the chairman was placed in a position where he could bring before the committee only those bills referred to it. As we know, such bills represent the opinion of the government. Despite the fact that members serving on the committee want to be non-partisan, and look at the matter in a reasonable way, they are placed in a position either where they have to go along completely with the government, as represented by the bills, or make a fight for it, with the result that the government and the opposition parties are divided in the committee.
I think this is a bad development. Further, the fact that the resolution has been on the order paper since February 11 indicates bad judgment on the part of someone in the government. I am not blaming the minister entirely because I know that he, too, is in the hands of the board of strategy and treasury board. The fact that the resolution has been on the order paper a long time has served as an aggravation to veterans organizations outside the House of Commons. They have been clamoring for amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. In the face of that fact we find placed on the order paper a motion to set up a committee, and the fact advertised that by that motion the very act that is agitating the veterans, the one they think needs amendment so badly, is omitted. The motion is left on the order paper for three months. It is just like waving a red rag at a bull. There is no doubt that that is why hon. members are receiving great numbers of resolutions and telegrams.
Several times in the house we have moved that the committee on veterans affairs should be a standing committee of the house, rather than having it as a committee to be called together by the government, if it sees fit. The government is under no obligation to take such action.
I believe the veterans affairs should be a standing committee. There is a motion on the order paper now which, if passed, would have the effect of making it a standing committee. And I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that

you will tell me I have no right in this debate to discuss a resolution on the order paper.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will tell my hon. friend that I would-if I did not know that there is no chance of reaching that particular order.

Thank you very much. It would seem that the rules are, after all, a bit flexible.
I have said that in my view the committee on veterans affairs should be a standing committee of the House of Commons. Surely the thousands of veterans who fought in the first and second world wars, who fought in Korea, who are now serving in Germany, and the hundreds more who are now in this country in uniform, prepared to offer their lives if necessary, are just as worthy of consideration as other matters which are discussed in standing committees. There comes to my mind the matter of transport-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: No.

No, perhaps not transport. However, there are sixteen standing committees of the house, including the committee on the restaurant, the library, divorce, miscellaneous private bills, and many other subjects. They are necessary, of course, although some of them never meet.
Do not hon. members feel that in the interests of the general welfare of the country, and in the light of the changing pattern in the services from year to year, it is necessary now that we have a standing committee of the house which, so far as possible, would consist of members who have served in the armed forces? I suggest he should be in a position whereby he could rise in his place and ask for the setting up of such a committee.
In this way it would be possible to have a continuous examination of veterans problems, and they would not be permitted to reach the state of turmoil we now find in connection with war veterans allowances. In the procedure I have suggested it would not be possible to set up a committee which would fail to deal with those matters about which the veterans have become agitated. I suggest the establishing of a standing committee would be helpful to the minister, because I am sure he knows there are many members in the house who are quite reasonable and who also have contact with veterans organizations. Let us keep in mind that the brains are not all in the civil service, the

fellows who draft these complicated amendments. If a standing committee were set up the minister would receive much valuable advice.
Let us not continue along the line now suggested, where we are developing a division of hon. members along political lines in the matter of veterans problems. Those problems have always been considered sacrosanct. I recall that for many years, indeed right up to 1939, any politician who attempted from a platform to raise controversial issues respecting veterans affairs did not generally get many votes. He was put in his place by any meeting where he attempted to raise a subject of that kind. That is the way we should keep it, because there should be no politics in matters having to do with veterans affairs.
When this committee begins to function it will not have very much to do. The bills that are to go before the committee are necessary adjustments to existing legislation, but there are not many changes in them. Changes in veterans legislation are necessary but they are not included in these bills. I am not going to discuss details now, but I have some opinions about the War Service Grants Act and the act respecting the Canadian forces as well as the other matters that have been referred to. Many things in veterans legislation need expanding, but this is not the time to do it.
I point out to the minister that his mediums of publicity are not good. For example, people outside this house and a lot of members in the house have always taken a dim view of casual earnings with respect to veterans allowances. I am not going to discuss the details of that except to tell the minister that this business of making changes in basic legislation by order in council and then issuing a directive based on that order in council does not get a very wide circulation, and that is responsible for a whole lot of misunderstanding that exists with respect to much of this legislation.
I met the parliamentary assistant to the minister the other day over a cup of coffee in the cafeteria, and he put me straight on something. Despite the fact that, as I said, a directive was sent out recently by the minister's department-I may as well give the number, W.V.A.B. No. 25-53-that pretty well revised the whole matter of casual earnings, I have been receiving letters on this subject and I did not know anything about it until I got a copy from the parliamentary assistant. I have given some publicity to it myself in my own area to bring it up to date. A lot of changes were made there, and they are good ones as far as they go. Quite a number of people were 83276-289
Committee on Veterans Affairs throwing rocks at the Department of Veterans Affairs on this v,ery matter. A lot of this trouble goes right back to the local districts. I am talking about my own now. They may be very efficient in other sections, but a lot of the difficulty over publicizing these changes from time to time goes right back to the local districts. Very little is known about it unless of course you walk into an office and sit down and discuss it with someone. I am merely leaving that thought with the minister. First, I do not agree with changing basic legislation by order in council in a matter as important as that affecting the casual earnings or parttime earnings of a recipient of veterans allowances. When a directive of that kind is issued it should go to the press in every part of the country. In addition to that, the district offices and the sub-district offices that enforce or handle that type of order should also be instructed to publicize it and see that all veterans who are entitled to the benefits because those changes are made are made acquainted with them.
In regard to the procedural question that came up, I am just going to say that because the War Veterans Allowance Act was not included in the terms of reference I, too, am very disappointed. I know from experience here that you cannot amend the terms of reference in the way that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) tried to amend it, but I still hope-we have a month and a half to go before the end of the session- that this committee-
The hon. member is a little optimistic, is he not?

The end of June. I hope that the committee that will be set up will be able to deal with this matter. I know the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) is just as anxious as we are to have the necessary amendments made to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and I hope that he will prevail upon the treasury board, and those who may be reluctant at this time to let us have a look at it, to permit the necessary amendments to that act and have it referred to the committee.
I could talk all afternoon on the reasons why this act should be amended, but I am not going to place Mr. Speaker in the position of having to declare me out of order. Before the minister closes this debate I would like him to clarify something in my own mind. This matter that I am now about to refer to is dealt with in one of the bills that we are to examine. Previous to the armistice in Korea, the Korean veterans were entitled to all the benefits that accrued

Committee on Veterans Affairs to veterans of world war II under our legislation. I have had many protests from different parts of the country to the effect that since the armistice was declared, by some decree on the part of the government, it was decided to discontinue the benefits such as gratuities and credits for Korean veterans as from the time of the armistice, and that relieving veterans who go to Korea from Canada are in the same position as the 27th brigade in Germany. If that is so-I am not sure it is except from the correspondence- in my judgment there is no justification for it, because there is no similarity of service as between the brigade in Germany and the troops in Korea. The troops in Germany are living under peacetime conditions, but the Korean troops are in a country that is completely devastated. They are living under war conditions at the present time. No one in this house or outside it can say that war in Korea is over. That has still to be determined. It is merely a cease-fire, and the duties they perform are in effect war duties. Their conditions, their circumstances, their recreation, their method of living, their housing in that part of the world bears no resemblance whatsoever to that of the troops in Germany. Since we are to deal with the Canadian forces and the legislation that should be applicable to them, I hope the minister and hon. members will keep in mind that that is a point we should work over pretty thoroughly, because the veterans organizations who have written to me about it have said emphatically that they consider it unjustifiable and completely rank discrimination as far as the Korean troops are concerned.
Hon. members are pretty restricted in this discussion, but the plea that I made to the minister at the beginning is that I hope he may be able to drive home to the government the fact that the method of setting up this committee, and its terms of reference, which say that only the legislation already determined by the government and passed to the committee in the form of a bill can be considered, are too restrictive. The government is completely disregarding the non-partisan spirit which existed in that committee previously. They are submitting bills for consideration by members of that committee, including members of the opposition who previously examined such questions on merit, bills which are designed to implement government policy and which will force these opposition members to think along political lines rather than attempt to maintain the nonpartisan spirit which existed previously. In my view the strength of the House of Commons in safeguarding the interests of veterans was concentrated in that committee due to


the impartial manner in which it considered veterans legislation. I hope the government may give serious consideration to making this a standing committee so that when problems arise from time to time, as they must during our lifetime, and which will affect veterans particularly in this changing world, the members of the house who are interested may be able to ask the minister to set up the committee to consider these problems rather than wait for someone in the government to determine in his judgment when veterans problems should be considered. It appears now that they not only determine when these problems should be handled, but they write the legislation and then throw it before the committee to fight over along partisan lines.
I think that is the most important aspect of the matter which confronts us at the present time and it is my belief that the government has neglected to place before that committee necessary amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. That act is the focal point in all problems affecting veterans today. Adjustments are necessary in other acts, but a change in the status of that committee from a veterans committee to a legislative examining committee which can act only on government legislation is very bad, and I trust that by the time we get around to dealing with veterans problems the minister will be in a position to announce that a standing committee of the house will be set up for the purpose of a continual review and survey of veterans problems as they arise from time to time.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this resolution designed to set up a committee on veterans affairs, but I feel I have to go along with the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in the view that during the last few years the committee on veterans affairs has drifted away from its original attitude and is not now concerned with a sincere discussion on veterans affairs. During the last three or four years we have not had the opportunity to thoroughly discuss the entire realm of veterans legislation, and I have found that the committee is what I might call a "me too" committee. The government suggests changes in the legislation; the committee talks it over; the government members of that committee say "me too"; the chairman says "me too"; he comes into the house and makes his report and the report says "me too"; the house then discusses it and the majority of hon. members in the house, of course, say "me too".
I too, Mr. Speaker, think that this committee on veterans affairs should be made

a standing committee of this house because it would appear that we are going to have veterans affairs problems for a good many years to come. We had the first world war; the second world war; then we had Korea; we have men in Germany; we have men in Korea, and there is a possibility of some sort of action in Indo-China. The United Nations' troops are carrying out police actions all over the world and members of our armed forces are travelling all over the world. We never know when we might be taking part in another war. That danger has often been underlined. We have a very delicate situation in Korea today, and with the international situation as it is we cannot avoid maintaining a strong standing army or at least carrying out a strong armed forces program. In the light of these facts we must have some sort of veterans organization within this house in order to keep pace with events.
I know it has been pointed out on many occasions that such a standing body is not necessary because we can always set up the veterans affairs committee, and it is asked, "Why set it up if we do not require it?" I wish the same sort of attitude could be taken with regard to some of the other standing committees. I have been a member of some of these committees for four years now, and they have not been called together and probably never will be, at least during my tenure of office. In spite of that, something that is as important, long lasting, and as near to us all the time as veterans legislation is ignored and we have to set up a veterans affairs committee whenever the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and the government decide that we should do so. This is not good enough. We need a permanent committee on veterans affairs which could be called together at any time to discuss matters arising in relation to veterans legislation.
Other hon. members have pointed out that this resolution has been on the order paper for something like two or two and one-half months, and I think it should have been brought before the house a long time ago. It is getting late in the session now. The minister has pointed out that he wishes to submit other legislation which will then be submitted to the veterans committee, but we still have not heard anything about that legislation and it has still to come before this house before it is submitted to the committee. In my opinion that legislation should have been introduced and brought before the committee on veterans affairs at least a month or two ago, because from now on all hon. members will be up to the ears in work with the estimates before us in this 83276-289J
Committee on Veterans Affairs chamber, and we are not going to have much opportunity to be absent in order to attend the sittings of the committee on veterans affairs. Sometimes I wonder if that is not the reason, and that this resolution was held over so that members of the veterans affairs committee would not be in the house to discuss the estimates of various departments.
As regards the terms of reference, I cannot help sharing the view of other hon. members who have already spoken on this topic. The terms of reference are much too narrow and I hope that if the minister does not see fit to extend the terms of reference we might at least be given sufficient leeway within that committee to discuss the entire realm of veterans affairs, and hear briefs from the various veterans organizations.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, on that particular subject I would like to know if the minister has invited veterans organizations to attend and present their views in the legislation which is to be submitted to this committee. As I was saying, I hope that we will have sufficient leeway to cover the whole field of veterans legislation because, in my opinion, veterans have been held down far too long, living at subnormal standards and being forced to merely exist when they should be living comfortably. For example, the Pension Act should be thoroughly overhauled and there should be a substantial upward revision in the amount paid to recipients.
I am not going to dig into the relative merits of the War Veterans Allowance Act. However, I may say that act was brought forward because it was said that the veteran preaged by at least ten years. I should like to tell the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) that many of these veterans are ageing extremely rapidly from trying to get along on the pittance the government is giving them at the present time.
As to the terms of reference, I do not think they should be laid down by the government. The members of the veterans affairs committee of the House of Commons are themselves veterans. The problems of the veteran are close to them and are matters of concern to them. I think the members of the committee are the ones who should determine just what its terms of reference are in order to be able to dig into all of this thing and to make a complete revision of the veterans legislation; it needs it. If this committee is going to be set up, let us leave it to that committee to do a job so as to give the veteran something instead of being set up just to look into some minute amendment which is brought down by the government, is introduced to a predominantly Liberal committee and which we

Committee on Veterans Affairs know is going to be passed as it was introduced to that committee, while all we can do, so far as the committee is concerned, is to blow off a little bit of steam and let people know exactly what we think.
