Mr. Speaker, I rise at this time to say a few words as one who has been on every veterans affairs committee of this house since 1935. Like every hon. member who has already spoken, I feel that this committee should be a standing committee and that it should be composed of a greater number of members than 31. It must be remembered that since 1945 we have had in this house a great number of veterans not only of the first great war but also of the second great war. A moment ago I mentioned that I had been on every veterans committee since 1935. I know that I am not being put on this committee this year. I could have been put on it but I voluntarily gave way to a younger member, a veteran of the second world war. Therefore, being deprived of the opportunity of again serving on this special veterans affairs committee, I felt that I should take part in this debate.
I certainly feel that it is a great mistake that this committee has been reduced, over the years, from some 60 members, when the veterans charter was discussed, until at the present time it numbers 31 members out of a house that contains possibly double the number of veterans it contained in 1945. I think it is a gross injustice to the veteran members of this house that the committee should be such a small one.
I also wish to say that I am greatly disappointed that amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act are not to be considered this year, and I know that veterans throughout Canada are also disappointed. As to the Veterans Land Act, which I believe is to be amended, I most certainly hope that the small holding limitation of two acres will be reduced. As I have said on many occasions in the past, half an acre is more than enough for any veteran to care for.
I have another matter that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, because I feel it is a matter that should be discussed by the veterans affairs committee this year. I realize that it might more appropriately be taken up by possibly another department, but it is a veterans problem and I feel that the Department of Veterans Affairs should press for immediate elimination of the difficulty. It is the case of a veteran who in applying for old age security is being denied it for several years because the time he spent overseas
[Mr Thomas.]

during the first world war is not allowed as residence in Canada. I fully realize that where an applicant has been a permanent resident in Canada for the entire 20 years, with a part of that unbroken 20 years spent overseas, it is allowed. But in this particular case to which I refer-and there have been similar cases-they run into the difficulty of not having resided in Canada for a long enough period to qualify. The point I wish to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, is that while the veteran is being denied the pension for some two years because his service overseas in the first great war was not allowed as residence in Canada, his wife, who remained in Canada while he was overseas, has been granted the pension. It was granted to her in April of this year, last month. The veteran who served overseas will not receive his pension until November of 1955. That is a point that I feel should be taken up by the minister. Perhaps I should not have raised it at this time but as I am not to be a member of the veterans affairs committee I felt that I should take the first opportunity to direct attention to it. I might say that this condition has been known by the minister of another department for several years. I would say that is one matter that should be taken up immediately and corrected. It could very well have been changed by an order in council. I sometimes wonder, Mr. Speaker, just how stupid people can get. I feel that it is a great injustice to a man who has served his king and country on the field of battle to be discriminated against to that extent; it certainly is a disgrace.
These are just a few remarks that I wished to make at this time. I want veterans generally and the members of this house to know that I am still just as much interested as ever in veterans affairs. As I said previously, however, I have relinquished my right to sit on that committee. Only six members were allocated to the Conservative party, and I have given my place to a younger man, a veteran of the second world war.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has pointed out, some of us have had a valuable lesson in pro"edure this afternoon. As a result of the rulings handed down by Your Honour I feel that I shall have to discard a good many of the notes I have here on the war veterans allowance. However, I should like to congratulate the minister and the government on bringing in this resolution to set up a committee on veterans affairs. While the personnel of the committee has not yet been announced, I am sure that every veteran

member of the house as well as every other member will watch with considerable interest the deliberations of this committee. Perhaps some day we can convince the minister that this committee should be a permanent one. I notice that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) asked for this concession. Then he proceeded to criticize the matters which are being referred to this committee in the resolution. I say to him that I think all changes in veterans legislation should be referred to this committee, whether those changes are large or small. Like other members who have spoken, I am disappointed that the matter of war veterans allowance was not specifically mentioned in the resolution. Perhaps the minister will yet bring this matter before the committee. I earnestly hope that he will although, as Your Honour has pointed out, hoping will not necessarily make it so. However, as I read the terms of reference of the committee there is scope there for the question of war veterans allowance to be brought before the committee before the session ends.
During my first speech in the house on November 26 last I urged the government to consider favourably the excellent brief presented last fall by the Canadian Legion, particularly that part relating to the war veterans allowance. In my opinion there are many reasons why an increase in the war veterans allowance is warranted at the present time, but I shall not attempt to go into them all. The case for the war veterans allowance recipients is well set out in the Legion brief for all to read. I still think they have a very strong case and I urgently commend it to the government for their further consideration.
There is a situation developing in my own province of Alberta at the present time involving recipients of war veterans allowance which is particularly serious. In our province, as in British Columbia, there is a supplementary old age pension allowance of $15 per month, bringing the total old age pension, with the means test of course, up to $55 per month for a single person. If a married couple both qualify they will receive together $110 per month. I should say at this stage that the additional $5 added to the additional $10 supplementary allowance will not be paid until the first of June and thereafter.
I am informed, Mr. Speaker, and I have no reason to doubt it, that there are many cases of persons in Alberta who are not even citizens, much less veterans, who will be receiving $110 per married couple per month as old age pensioners. Such persons may even have fought against us in world war I, but they will still receive old age assistance in
Committee on Veterans Affairs the amount I have indicated provided that they qualify by having resided in Canada for twenty years or more and can pass the means test. I am not suggesting for one moment that these needy people are receiving too much by way of assistance, but the situation I have outlined does point up the urgent need for some revision of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
On the other hand, war veterans allowance recipients who also qualify for the old age pension-and I already have a letter from one such person-are limited to $100 per month under the $1,200 per year maximum permissible income ceiling. Surely this is not fair to our aged veterans who, incidentally, had to see service in an actual theatre of war in order to qualify for war veterans allowance. I think I should also point out that there is a war veterans allowance assistance fund up to $15 per month for those who are in dire need. I simply want to point out to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) the situation that is developing in Alberta and ask him to look into the matter very closely in order to make sure that our war veteran recipients in that province do not come out second best.
Of course I realize that the federal government cannot always be changing its policies because of the actions from time to time of various provincial legislatures, but at the same time the situation I have outlined with respect to the recipients of war veterans allowance is one that should not be allowed to persist indefinitely. Because of the rigorous means test prescribed, I am not afraid of the war veterans allowance going to people who do not need it and who do not deserve it, but I am very much concerned about whether those in need are getting a square deal, and I am confident that the government shares that view. I can only repeat what I said in the house on November 26 last, that in my opinion both the basic rate and the permissible income figures for the war veterans allowance are too low at the present time.
Having said that, I must in all fairness add something more. First of all I should like to say that I have great confidence in the Minister of Veterans Affairs, as I had in his predecessors. Between them they have done an outstanding job for the veterans of Canada. I think it is generally agreed that the treatment this government has meted out to Canada's war veterans is without equal in any other country in the world. The veterans charter of Canada, as we call it, has never been equalled anywhere, much less surpassed. Almost literally our war veterans have been looked after in a hundred and one different ways. This is only as it

Committee on Veterans Affairs should be. They have not received too much for no amount of assistance would repay or compensate them for what they have sacrificed for Canada. By their actions they have brought victory and freedom, unity and strength, not to speak of fame and glory, to our beloved country.
But the government has not forgotten these veterans. In Saturday's paper we read that the government is spending $127 million a year in war disability pensions alone. On top of this, the government is spending some $26 million in war veterans allowances each year. The newspaper article pointed out that this was in the order of $242 per minute for disability pensions or, if the war veterans allowance is included, we have a figure of approximately $290 per minute being spent by Canada in veterans pensions and allowances. But this only covers two items of veterans legislation. Actually hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested and are being invested in many other forms of veterans rehabilitation.
I appreciate that the government feels that the line must be drawn somewhere. Theirs is the responsibility of seeing that the country, in all its aspects, is run in a manner that seems to them to be in the best interests of Canada as a whole. But in my opinion the government is hewing too close to the line in the matter of the war veterans allowances. It will be my endeavour to try to persuade the government, as I am now doing, to reconsider this particular matter. As I have said, I have confidence in the Minister of Veterans Affairs and in the government. One has only to study the veterans charter to find ample reason for that confidence. Already in this session amendments to the veterans charter have been introduced in favour of the war veterans in several different respects. More amendments are to be brought in at this session, as the minister has indicated today. I am sure that these amendments will prove to be of further assistance to the men and women who have fought Canada's battles in the past.
I am particularly interested in the amendments to the Veterans Land Act that the minister is going to introduce. Having had the privilege of serving with the Veterans Land Act administration for seven years I know what a tremendous benefit the provisions of that act have been to our farmer, fisherman and small holder veterans, and I think any amendments to that act will be further well earned assistance to these veterans. Judging by what the government has done for our veterans since 1945, 1 have every confidence that they will continue to do the right thing by those who have done


so much for Canada. To our war veterans no sacrifice was too great when Canada needed sacrifice. Therefore I urge the government to take another look at the matter of the war veterans allowance. I hope that they will do this and come forward with a proposal for an increase in both the basic rates and the permissible income ceiling. As I have said before, there is scope in the resolution for such amendments, and I still have hopes that something will be done about it at the present session of parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I have noticed that so far every speaker, irrespective of the party to which he belongs, has referred to the particular resolution before us as being too confining in its nature. I agree with them 100 per cent. It is thirty-five years since the first war ended and there are problems affecting the veterans of that war that are still unsettled. There is nobody to which they can come to have those problems aired in a proper manner. I do not feel that the paid officials, who are there to administer the act, are the right people with whom to discuss proposed changes in the act. The veterans themselves or the veteran members of the house should have some say in the matter. Since these problems have remained unsolved, as they have for thirty-five years, it is time a change was made in the method of dealing with them. I feel that in this particular instance the reference to the committee should cover all veterans problems.
The veterans themselves had some hope that when the committee was set up it would deal with all their problems, and particularly veterans allowances. These problems have been brought to the attention of the government, and it is a slap in the face to the veteran and the veterans organizations who have consistently asked for the opportunity to discuss veterans allowances, that this matter is not to be considered.
I agree with the member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) that we should have a standing committee on veterans affairs. As a matter of fact, on December 9 last I had the following proposed resolution put on the order paper:
That standing order 63 be amended by inserting therein immediately after subsection (1) the following new subsection:
(m) on veterans affairs, to consist of 35 members, 10 of whom shall constitute a quorum.
This idea is not entirely my own, but is general throughout Canada. An opportunity for airing the grievances that are continuously being brought up through veterans organizations and directly to the member of parliament by the veterans themselves ought

to be provided. I feel it would eliminate a great deal of dissatisfaction that we have at the present time. It would eliminate dissatisfaction with what the department calls borderline cases, because in most instances the department takes the line most favourable to the government. This happens in spite of the fact that time and time again we have been told the veteran will be given the benefit of the doubt. I can prove that in some instances such has not been the case. I feel that such a committee would be of immense help to the minister. Through the members the minister could be kept up to date on conditions throughout the country.
There is no family in the whole dominion that is not, in some way, touched by veterans problems, either through the husband, son, daughter or other relative who served in one of the forces. The importance of this subject is so widespread that I feel a standing committee should be set up immediately. The recent sittings of the agriculture committee have been of interest to me. This committee had to consider the report of the Canadian wheat board, which was placed before the committee in its entirety as well as the recommendations resulting from the year's operation. Members of the board were there to answer questions. I thought the idea was a good one because the matter was dealt with by a group who understood wheat problems and who understood what they were doing about them. This arrangement proved very satisfactory. I believe that the committee that is now being set up for veterans affairs should be asked to consider the Canadian Legion brief in its entirety, as presented to the government last November 10, just as the agriculture committee considered a brief that was not sponsored by a minister of the crown.
I feel that in that way we could deal much more satisfactorily with the problems so far as the veterans are concerned. These problems go beyond the bills referred to the committee. These bills hardly go anywhere at all, but merely remedy one or two little things the minister feels should be remedied. I feel this brief was prepared by a body in much closer touch with the needs of veterans than those who administer the act in Ottawa would be. I should like to comment upon one or two aspects of the brief, but in view of Mr. Speaker's ruling I shall satisfy myself by mentioning the need for revision of veterans allowances. This brief contains suggested remedies for the protection of these veterans. I could give instance after instance which I hope I shall be able to do later in the session, illustrating the injustices created
Committee on Veterans Affairs by the administration of this act-I am speaking of the veterans allowances now.
There are other recommendations in the brief equally as important concerning veterans who live outside of Canada. These veterans are few in number, so the cost would not be very great if the minister acceded to their request. In many cases, these men must live outside of Canada for health reasons.
Another point that I think is important, and I have taken it up with the department, is the arbitrary way in which a veteran's allowance is affected by his earnings on a ranch. I have several veterans on small holdings in the Okanagan. I know of one whose income from operations was just about $1,000, but his total operating costs-he is a cripple- were over $1,200. He showed a net loss for the year of $200, but under the new ruling the department said, no, 50 per cent of your gross must be regarded as net profit. In his case, as a result, he and his wife had about $21 per month on which to live. I feel that such matters as that should be dealt with by the standing committee. I have cited one example and could go on to others. There are several others who have been treated in the same way.
The other matter that I believe is urgent concerns widows' pensions. I have mentioned the subject before, but I am going to do it again because the departmental ruling is still the same. If a disabled pensioner dies while receiving only 49 per cent or less, the widow gets nothing. If he received 50 per cent or more, the widow gets a substantial pension. I claim that the line is too hard and fast. It would not cost the government any money because it would merely be a continuation of the pension received by the husband before he died. He would have been paid had he lived, so it is a continuation of a part of the pension to the widow after he has died. Such action would remove a condition that is very unfair, especially if the matter was discussed in the proposed committee. Without going into detail, I would suggest to the minister that he again review the Canadian Legion brief and see if he cannot agree with me that it is a comprehensive one produced by experts in the field of veterans affairs and presented fairly and truthfully. If that brief were presented to the committee, with a request for recommendations, I believe the minister could be satisfied that veterans problems were on the road to being solved.
I would point out that it is the duty of every member of the house, and particularly veteran members, to deal with veterans' problems. If we cannot get that opportunity we are frustrated, the Legion is frustrated,

Committee on Veterans Affairs the veterans are frustrated and everyone is frustrated in presenting veterans problems. Today we have seen an attempt made to curtail the discussion of this vital subject. The day may yet come when we shall want to call upon the young people of Canada to fight our battles in perhaps still another war. If the treatment accorded the veterans of the three previous wars is not satisfactory, there will be little chance of being successful in the recruiting program for the next war. I think to a certain extent that is the reason recruiting today is 25 per cent less than the target set for last month by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton).
I hope the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) will take heed of what has been said by hon. members and, before it is too late, either suggest a standing committee on veterans affairs or enlarge immediately the scope of the committee now to be set up.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members are pleased that this committee is to be set up again at the present session. We do regret however that the time of the session is fast running out, and we can see no particular reason why the resolution could not have been presented to the house earlier in order that the committee might have had ample time to cover the work now placed before it. We cannot help that; but the fact remains that the motion to set up the committee has been put off time after time, indicating to me that perhaps the minister was waiting for some representation or other in order to make an important decision.
However, the resolution is now before us, and all hon. members are pleased that the committee is to be set up. We have reason to congratulate previous committees on the work they have done over the years. I do not know that I can agree altogether with the suggestion that the committee is deteriorating. It may be that I have not paid sufficient attention to it. Some members have made reference to this suggestion, but I can see no reason why the effectiveness of the committee should deteriorate in any way. I believe if we have the proper men on the committee it will do admirable work.
While at times we may appear critical of veterans legislation, compared with the legislation brought down immediately after the first world war, I am sure the veterans of the second world war have reason to believe that they have been treated with a high degree of consideration. I was talking to a veteran of the first world war, one who is


now growing older and has become a successful businessman, who indicated to me that veterans returning from the first world war would have been mighty glad to have had the privileges and opportunities afforded those returning from the second. He did admit that veterans of the first world war are now covered by various forms of legislation which apply also to those of the second world war.
A good deal has been said this afternoon about the terms of reference to the committee, and the suggestion is made that they are not wide enough in scope. I agree with what has been said in this connection, recognizing always the fact that we cannot go into a discussion of the missing piece of legislation, namely, the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am reminded by my leader however that a previous speaker created a precedent by discussing that matter. I am not going to follow his example, but shall state briefly that the fact the War Veterans Allowance Act is not included will be a source of great disappointment to many veterans, particularly those of the first world war who feel that further consideration should be given to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and certain necessary changes made in it.
The fact that the resolution has been on the order paper for so long has given a good deal of hope to these older veterans. They have been waiting in the expectation and anticipation that something more was going to be done for them.
There is a class of people in Canada today who are seriously neglected. I refer not only to the older war veterans but also to their widows-women who have passed the age where they can find suitable employment. To my mind they are more or less a forgotten class. I am not saying they are not properly dealt with where the legislation covers them; I know the officials want to do all they can for them under that legislation, but the fact is that the legislation does not go far enough. I suggest that the terms of reference to the committee should have been wide enough to have permitted it to study this matter and to make recommendations in the matter of war veterans allowances.
An amendment has been moved previously and declared by you, Mr. Speaker, to be out of order. In the light of the fact that it referred to the inclusion in the resolution of a specific act, and the further fact that Your Honour cited many previous decisions, I am afraid we will have to concur in your ruling. However I have here an amendment that I believe covers the point and is also in order. Otherwise I would not present it

I do present it because I believe the committee should be master in its own household. If it so desires it should be able to discuss other matters that it might consider should be discussed.
Therefore I move the following amendment, and I suggest it is only a slight one:
That the sentence, "and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee" be deleted, and the following substituted therefor:
"and such other matters relating to veterans affairs as the committee may decide."
The resolution would then read:
Resolved that a special committee consisting of thirty-one members, to be designated by the house at a later date, be appointed to consider the bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and the bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces, and such other matters relating to veterans affairs as the committee may decide; that the said committee shall have power to send for persons, papers, and records, to print from day to day its minutes of proceedings and evidence, to sit while the house is sitting and to report from time to time; that the quorum of the said committee shall consist of ten members; and that the provisions of standing orders 64 and 65 be suspended in relation thereto.
That will not harm the resolution in any way. It will not prevent any other matter being referred to it. It will also make the committee freer to go into a discussion of all matters relating to veterans affairs, as the committee itself may decide.
I move this amendment, Mr. Speaker, and commend it to the consideration of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order; may I draw your attention to the rulings that have been discussed this afternoon at some length? The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) has felt that in wording the amendment as he has he has shifted the onus to the committee and thereby from the house. It is the house, however, that sets the terms of the appointment of the committee, and its terms of reference. I think my hon. friend is in the same difficulty that any other amendment might be in because of the ruling made in 1951 which has been referred to, as I say, on more than one occasion. May I read very briefly from the ruling? It had to do with the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks):
Mr. Speaker ruled the proposed amendment out of order on the ground that an amendment cannot be moved giving the committee wider powers than those which were set out in the notice of motion.
I suppose my hon. friend can say that this amendment does not extend the powers of the committee; that the committee itself might decide that it would not consider any legislation except that referred to in the 83276-290
Covimittee on Veterans Affairs original notice of motion. But since he gives them power to do so, I think we ought to assume that they would exercise it, and for that reason it is extending the scope of the motion of which notice was given in the proper manner. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I understand that previously this afternoon Mr. Speaker ruled an amendment by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) out of order, and I believe he cited at that time several decisions, one of which will be found in the Journals of 1951, at page 243, and the other of which will be found in the Journals of 1952, at page 240. In each case the amendments to a similar motion as that under consideration at this time were ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker on the ground:
. . . that an amendment cannot be moved giving the committee wider powers than those which were set out in the notice of motion.
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for Macleod would add the following words to the motion:
and such other matters relating to veterans affairs as the committee may decide.
Should the word "matters" refer to legislation, then under the terms of the original motion, which refers to certain specific legislation which will be referred to the committee and certain other legislation which may be referred to the committee, in my opinion the amendment is a nullity and would be out of order.
On the other hand, if the word "matters" refers to things other than legislation, then I can only feel that the effect of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Macleod would be to widen the powers of the committee, and as any such widening of powers under the rulings previously cited has been ruled out of order by Mr. Speaker, I believe that I can only rule the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Macleod out of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that this resolution to set up a special committee on veterans affairs has at long last been moved. It is difficult for me to understand why it has been sitting on the order paper for three months instead of having been moved shortly after it first appeared. As a result of it having been delayed for this three months' period I am afraid that the work of the veterans committee will now be rushed in a way which is not at all necessary.

Committee on Veterans Affairs
Possibly the reason for the motion not being moved earlier was the fact that these matters that are specifically referred to it are not matters which are going to take a great deal of time and are not matters on which there is going to be a great deal of disagreement. As was stated by the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks), to some extent they are almost what you might call routine matters; extension of veterans benefits enjoyed by people in the second great war particularly to those who served in the Korean war. Therefore possibly the reason that this motion stood so long on the order paper is that the government was determined not to have some of the matters with which veterans are more concerned at the present time, such as war veterans allowances, dealt with in the committee.
I was extremely sorry that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Royal was ruled out of order, and also the amendment just moved by the hon. member for Macleod. There is no question that the matter about which veterans are more concerned than any other is the rates of war veterans allowances and the allowable earnings which the recipients of war veterans allowances can receive. It is the most pressing veterans' question we have, and it is the one above all others which this committee now being set up should consider.
It would appear that the terms of reference are quite narrow, and that has been the case in the last two or three veterans committees that have been set up. I think it is a great mistake, as nearly every hon. member who has taken part in this debate today has also said. In spite of the fact that war veterans allowance is not specifically mentioned in this resolution, I would hope that the committee will be able to discuss it. That, as a matter of fact, was the situation in one committee.
It was not specifically mentioned in the terms of reference of a committee of two or three years ago, but veterans organizations, the Legion, the navy, army and air force veterans, and others appearing before the committee, made recommendations in regard to war veterans allowance, pension matters and other matters, and as a result of our discussing these questions with those veterans representatives, the matter of war veterans allowance was discussed, although it was not in the terms of reference. I would hope that the same thing might take place in this year's committee. I certainly hope that it will because if the committee is set up and is not ready to devote any time or give any consideration to improving the matter of war veterans allowance it will not do the job

which the veterans of this country expect it to do. It will prove to be a great disappointment to Canadian veterans.
Now, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) made a strong plea for an improvement in the war veterans' allowance, and he said he was fully confident the government shared his views in that regard. But I am afraid the government's statements and actions so far this session do not justify that confidence. I hope the hon. member is correct, and I hope it is the government's view that improvements require to be made in the amount of payment under war veterans allowance and the amount of earnings veterans are allowed to make should be increased. I hope other hon. members on the government side who believe this action should be taken will put sufficient pressure on the government so that this matter may be referred to the veterans affairs committee and that some legislation will be brought in to cover these points.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) dealt with the legislation which is still to be introduced at this session a few days ago, and I was extremely disappointed that he made no mention whatever of war veterans allowances. As I have already pointed out, it is a matter of very pressing concern and one in which I believe nearly all hon. members in the house feel the government should make concessions so that the necessary amendment will be brought into the War Veterans Allowance Act to improve it in the two particulars I have mentioned.

serious consideration to amending the regulations-the resolution says the act; I understand it is the regulations-so that a veteran may acquire a small holding provided he can obtain half an acre of suitable land.
There is one other resolution which is extremely interesting because there are several cases of this type which have arisen in my constituency. This is a resolution that deals with the necessity of protecting the wife of a veteran who has purchased a home under the small holdings section of the Veterans Land Act. We have had two or three cases where the husband and wife have worked together since the war to obtain a small holding and build a home, then the husband has failed to live up to his responsibility and the poor wife, although she has done her best to build up the estate and has worked hard, was left high and dry because she has no legal interest in the property. It was on that account that the Nelson branch of the Canadian Legion adopted this resolution, which I commend to the minister for his consideration:
Whereas under the existing agreement made between the director of the Veterans Land Act and the veteran, the wife of the veteran is not protected in the event of desertion, as under the wives' protection act.
And whereas in the event of desertion by her husband she may be forced to vacate the property which she has helped to build up.
Therefore be it resolved that this convention strongly appeal for a revision of the Veterans Land Act, to permit joint ownership, which would provide protection for the wife.
I am not quite sure, Mr. Speaker, whether the remedy suggested there is the best one from a legal point of view, but I bring the resolution to the attention of the minister in the hope that something will be done to protect those unfortunate women who have made a joint contribution with a veteran to the building of a home. Fortunately these cases are few and far between, but where they occur they are the cause-and I say this from my personal knowledge-of considerable hardship on the wife concerned.
Like others who have spoken, Mr. Speaker, I greatly regret that the government has not paid attention to the repeated suggestions of the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations in Canada for an increase in the war veterans allowance. We all know that we have without a doubt the finest veterans legislation to be found anywhere in the democratic world. I think there is no question about that fact. Being a member of the committee I have had the opportunity, as have other hon. members, of studying the legislation passed in Great Britain, the United States, Norway, Finland, Denmark, Belgium,

France, New Zealand and Australia. After an extensive study of legislation passed on behalf of veterans and their dependents in other countries, I think it is quite fair to say that Canada can proudly say she has the best veterans legislation in the world. I therefore think it is rather unfortunate that we have failed to remove one or two illiberal blots on the legislation at this time.
Along with others who have spoken, I regret that the government has not seen fit- as was said by the hon. member for Edmon-ton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna)-to send to the committee a bill which would provide for amendment of the War Veterans Allowance Act so as to increase the war veterans allowance and hence make the lives of a number of veterans and their dependents much happier. As a result of this debate and as a result of public opinion in the country I hope that before this session ends the government will respond to our pleas and representations.
In conclusion I want to say a word or two about the committee. I think it is quite fair to say-and I am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton South will back me up in this statement-that throughout the years, generally speaking, the approach of the members of the veterans affairs committee has been a non-partisan one. I have found that to be the situation. Even government members on the committee, when they find that the government cannot be moved to do what the opposition members have been suggesting and what they themselves have suggested on occasion, feel quite uncomfortable about it. I must say that the tone of the debates in the committee and the working of it have been non-partisan. The colonel from Royal, the burly and rugged coal miner from Cape Breton South, that gentlemanly representative of the legal profession from Vancouver-Quadra, and the peasant farmer from Kootenay West all had one thing in common and one spirit. They look forward, as usual, to the spirit and tradition of the veterans affairs committee being carried on. That tradition and spirit is that we work together for the welfare of the veterans and their dependents.

Mr. Speaker, it is significant that every hon. member who has spoken in this debate, after the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), has shown grave concern that this committee which is to be set up will not have the power to deal with the War Veterans Allowance Act. I personally feel that a great injustice is being done to these front-line veterans who either are now qualified for that allowance or may become qualified before there is a suitable change in the act. I hope to place before the Minister of Veterans
Committee on Veterans Affairs Affairs, and more particularly before the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who is now in the house, a few words which will have some effect; I am optimistic enough to hope that the government will take another look at this question.
These special committees on veterans affairs are only set up occasionally. Time and again the request is made that there should be a standing committee to deal with these subjects but, as we all know, that request has been turned down. Once, twice, perhaps three times in a parliament, a special committee is set up to consider veterans affairs. The resolution we are considering today will set up the first committee of the present parliament on that subject. It is possible that there will not be another committee on veterans affairs during the whole life of this parliament. The setting up of this committee is extremely important, far more so I believe than is the case with any other special committee of the house.
As has been pointed out, the terms of reference are limited; they refer only to legislation. In the first place they mention two bills which have already been given second reading, a bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and a bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces. Then the terms of reference go on to refer to "such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee".
When the Prime Minister spoke on April 30 he gave the house a list of the legislation to be introduced before the end of the present session. The only bill in that list that affected veterans affairs was one to amend the Veterans Land Act. There is also of course a bill to amend the Pension Act already standing on the order paper which obviously will be referred to the committee. Therefore the present position is that we can expect to have only two more bills for consideration by the special committee. On the same day the Prime Minister was asked about the possibility of amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act. The question and answer will be found at page 4276 of Hansard of April 30. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) asked the following question:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister if he has not forgotten to bring in an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act. X am sure there will be great disappointment if no amendments to that act are brought in at this session.
The Prime Minister answered that question as follows:
I have stated a complete list of the government's program for the remainder of the session.
4574	HOUSE OF
Committee on Veterans Affairs
It is perfectly obvious therefore that unless there is a change of mind on the part of the cabinet there will be no bill to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session and therefore the special committee, under its terms of reference, cannot consider the question whether or not the present War Veterans Allowance Act is adequate. That, I am sure, is contrary to the expectations of veterans from one coast of Canada to the other. I have here a press dispatch reporting on a letter written by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) which shows that he too expected that this subject would be considered by the special committee. In Vancouver quite a campaign has been carried on with respect to the question of war veterans allowances by the West End branch of the Canadian Legion. Reports of their activities have appeared in a district paper known as the West Ender each week. I have here a copy of that paper for March 17 which contains this report concerning a letter written by the Minister of Finance:
Canada's finance minister, Hon. D. C. Abbott, is a very busy man but he took a few minutes to reply to our petition in behalf of the W.V.A. pensioners. Mr. Abbott states that veterans problems are under continuous study by the veterans affairs department, and legislation providing benefits are continuously reviewed. In conclusion he adds-
This is the part I wish to emphasize.
-that all due consideration will be given to W.V.A. recipients and that the problem will come before the special committee on veterans affairs to be set up during this session.
You see, Mr. Speaker, this question of the war veterans allowance is far and away the most important question worrying the Veterans of Canada today. It is of course of concern to every war veteran who is interested at all in veterans problems, and to the great veterans organizations of Canada. For example, when the Canadian Legion appeared before the cabinet in November of last year their first and main submission had to do with the war veterans allowance. I have no doubt the Prime Minister was present at that interview and that he will remember that the Legion placed the greatest emphasis on the need for amendment of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
It has also been the most important question concerning veterans affairs in this house. It was considered at great length and with some care by the last special committee on veterans affairs which met in 1952. I draw to the attention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Veterans Affairs the recommendation which finally came out of the special committee in 1952 respecting war veterans allowance. It was a unanimous recommendation; in fact, it was moved by the members of the Prime Minister's own
IMr. Green.]

party. Members of the opposition had previously moved a stronger recommendation but it was voted down. Then the Liberal members on the veterans affairs committee brought in this recommendation which was passed unanimously. It read as follows:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans organizations in that respect-
It will be noticed that here the committee picked out one particular point.
-and particularly with regard to permissive income.
In practically every other case in my memory where there has been a recommendation from a special committee on veterans affairs it has been acted upon by the government, usually during the same session. It is two years ago that this recommendation was made and yet the government has never acted.
1	do not say that the government failed to consider the question, but if the cabinet did consider it at all they obviously turned down the recommendation of the committee. Putting the matter on the basis of fairness to a committee of this house, on the basis that a committee of this house just two years ago made a definite recommendation for consideration of the need of amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act, I suggest that ihe committee now being set up should be given the power to consider this question even though the government is not prepared at the moment to take any action by way of introducing an amendment.
The committee could hear from the department. No doubt there is a story to be told by the department with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act. No doubt the officials would say that a special new provision was written into the act in 1952 which took care of many war veterans allowance recipients. However, I have here a return tabled for the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) giving the number of veterans who have benefited by reason of that change as of the 31st of October, 1953. They only amounted to 761 out of a total of 31,234. In other words, just slightly over
2	per cent of the recipients of war veterans al owance at that time were able to take advantage of the amendment which was put into the act in 1952.
This committee could hear from the veterans organizations. Surely, we are not to be put in the position where they are called before that committee but are not allowed to make any recommendations concerning war veterans allowances. I repeat that is the main problem facing the veterans

of Canada today. If the veterans organizations are allowed to make submissions, but the committee cannot make any recommendations, where is the sense of the committee being in that position? I suggest the committee should be given the power to deal with this question, to hear representations and to make recommendations to the house just as it did in 1952. If the government does not see fit to accept those recommendations, then that of course will be the responsibility of the government, as it ought to be.
This action of setting up a committee and depriving it of the power to deal with the main veterans problem amounts, in effect, to putting a lid on the problems that are worrying the veterans at the present time. In fact, it amounts to making this veterans affairs committee nothing more nor less than a rubber stamp to approve the four bills introduced by the government, and with practically all the terms of which everyone is in agreement. The work of the committee is reduced to such an extent it is hardly worth while setting up a committee at all.
I am not going to go into the reasons why the War Veterans Allowance Act should be amended. I believe they are well known to every member on the government side, just as they are to every member on this side. This afternoon I was struck by one fact brought out by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna). Incidentally, he is the only government supporter who has spoken in this debate, outside of the minister. This hon. member had the courage to say he thought this question should be faced at this session. He pointed out that now in Alberta a civilian can get an old age security payment from the dominion of $40, and an additional $15 from the province, whereas a veteran of course is limited to a total of $50.
The same situation exists in my own province of British Columbia. There have been amendments this year that have changed the law so that now a civilian, even a man who served in the German army and came to British Columbia afterwards, can now get $55 a month, whereas a man who was fighting in the front lines for Canada can only get $50 under the War Veterans Allowance Act. There is also the fact that the permissive income is only $10 a month, both in the case of a single veteran and of a married veteran. This is absolutely unfair. When the veteran reaches 70 and becomes eligible for old age security he cannot get the full $40 like everyone else in Canada. He is discriminated against because the ceiling on his permissive income is so low. However,
Committee on Veterans Affairs this is not the time to go into these details. They are bad enough, but I think everyone here knows about them.
It seems obvious that the veteran is being put on the basis of a welfare case. The war veterans allowance recipient is being treated the same as a civilian welfare case. It is for that reason we cannot get any improvement in the situation, and The Legionary put that quite clearly in the January edition in an article entitled "1953 in Retrospect":
Time and again we have been told by the Prime Minister and members of the cabinet that war veterans allowance rates and ceilings cannot be permitted to get too far out of line with other social benefits such as old age pensions, pensions for the blind, etc. Time and again we have pointed out that citizens of Canada are not required to render any special service to this country in order to become eligible for the usual social benefits available to all under certain conditions. On the other hand the veteran, before becoming eligible for war veterans allowance, must have served in a theatre of actual war and we are satisfied that the Canadian people would in consequence place him in a preferred position.
Leaving the act as it is means that the government is ignoring the fact that this is a claim by the veteran for services rendered. It is in the nature of a debt owing him by his country, and I believe is recognized as such by the Canadian people even if it is not so recognized by the government.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, to the private members on the government side of the house that they could force the government to introduce amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act during this session if they took a stand in this debate today. This is the time to do it. Do they believe that the War Veterans Allowance Act should be amended at this session or do they not? If they do, let them stand up and indicate to the government what they think should be done. Every single member on the opposition side, no matter to what party he or she may belong, stands firmly for changes in this act, and stands firmly for the veterans problems being aired in the special committee on veterans affairs. I believe most members on the government side feel the same way. I would hope that the Prime Minister would make his supporters feel free to express their opinions on this question rather than make it a party matter. Surely where the vast majority of the members here who have been elected by the people of Canada believe some action should be taken, the government should not make them go against what they feel on such a question.
I do not doubt that practically every member here today, including the members of the cabinet, told the veterans last year that this War Veterans Allowance Act would be

Committee on Veterans Affairs amended. I do not think there are many here who did not take that stand in the election just one year ago. This is the time to act. I hope this parliament will not put itself in the position of raising the pay of members and senators, then two or three weeks from now of every judge in Canada, but not giving any help to these front-line veterans. They have a far greater right to consideration than anyone in this house or in the Senate or on the bench in this land. Now is the time to see that they are given that consideration to which they are so fully entitled.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether I might correct the misinterpretation placed on my remarks by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness). I am sorry he is not in the house at the present time. I was out of my seat for a few moments this afternoon, and I am informed the hon. member told the house I had said I was confident that the government shared my view in the matter of war veterans allowances. That is not what I said. I am not confident that the minister shares my view, although I hope he does. I was speaking particularly of a situation that is likely to develop in Alberta where veteran old age pensioners may receive $10 a month less, as a couple, or $5 a month less for a single person than does a non-veteran old age pensioner. I had intended to say I was confident that the government would share my view that the veterans who are pensioners in Alberta should not be placed in a less advantageous position than non-veteran old age pensioners.
In other words, you have lost confidence in the government.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, whatever confidence or lack of confidence the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) may have in the government, I dare to believe that most private members on the government side of the house are still hoping that before this session ends something will be done with respect to the War Veterans Allowance Act. It seems to me that the way in which the ball might be started rolling in connection with this important question would be for the government to agree to an enlargement of the terms of reference of this motion so that this important question might be discussed by the special committee to be established when this motion passes.
Most hon. members who have spoken this afternoon have referred to this motion as one for the appointment of a committee on veterans affairs. I suppose there is a sense


in which that is the correct terminology. But I am inclined to agree with the view expressed by my colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), when he says that this is not a committee on veterans affairs in the sense in which we have known those committees in years gone by.
I recognize that when the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) announced to the house on February 11 that he was going to place a motion on the order paper he used these words:
It is therefore proposed to set up a special committee on veterans affairs this session.
But I suggest-and in this I do not think I am just being technical or legalistic-that this is not a motion to set up a committee on veterans affairs at all; this is a motion to set up a committee to which will be referred three bills. Two of those bills are named in the motion-a bill to amend the War Service Grants Act and a second one respecting the benefits for members of the Canadian forces. The third bill, as we know from what we have been told on other occasions, will be one to amend the Veterans Land Act.
Members supporting the government may argue that this is, in effect, a veterans affairs committee because the bills with which it will be dealing are bills relating to veterans affairs. But the committee suggested is not a veterans affairs committee as the House of Commons has known it in the past. And I must congratulate the Minister of Veterans Affairs upon not having tried to say in the wording of his motion that this is a veterans affairs committee. It is just a special committee to deal with three bills the government has decided should be referred to such a special committee. It is not a committee to go into the broad question of what our veterans in Canada need at the present time, as previous veterans affairs committees have been permitted to do.
I feel strongly that the whole question of the terms of reference of the committee should be reconsidered. I would hope that the Prime Minister, who has listened to all the appeals that have been made this afternoon, might reconsider the terms of reference. I would hope that the strong appeal made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) might lead the Prime Minister to reconsider this whole question.
As I indicated earlier, I could not but go along with Your Honour's attitude toward the amendments that were made, so far as the procedural position is concerned; but it is still possible for the government to respond to the wishes of the house and to ask the consent of the house to change the terms of this motion.

Since it is not possible to move an amendment asking for the inclusion of other matters such as the War Veterans Allowance Act, it is therefore not possible at this time to get a vote on that specific question by itself. Perhaps that is one reason that there may be more speakers in this debate than might otherwise be the case, because members generally in all parts of the house feel so keenly on this issue that they are anxious to express their views.
So far, as has been pointed out, apart from the minister who introduced the motion, we have heard only one speaker from the government side of the house, the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona. I hope there may be other speakers. Indeed I am waiting anxiously to hear from the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott). On February 11, when the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced that it was his intention to file notice of a motion for the setting up of this committee, the hon. member for Vancouver South made a very short speech in which he expressed his pleasure at this announcement. He even went on to say that this would now give him an answer to the 427 postcards that were lying on his desk upstairs. I would like to know what answer he gave on that occasion to those 427 postcards, and I would like to know further whether he has amended that answer.
When one reads the very brief statement the hon. member for Vancouver South made on that occasion it becomes quite clear he had confidence that the bringing down of a motion for the setting up of this committee meant that consideration was going to be given at this session to amending the War Veterans Allowance Act. As I say, now that he knows it is the government's intention that that matter shall not be referred to the committee, and that there shall not be a bill amending the War Veterans Allowance Act, I am wondering what amendment he is sending out to the answers he gave to the 427 veterans who sent him the postcards.
I have referred to the hon. member for Vancouver South, not to be critical of him for the view he expressed on February 11, because the same view was expressed by members in all parties. We were delighted with the announcement. It came as a surprise, right in the midst of another debate. I repeat that we were delighted with the announcement that a special committee on veterans affairs was to be established. What we are now disappointed in is that we are not getting a special committee on veterans affairs; we are getting merely a committee to consider three bills and nothing more. The terms of reference are limited, so limited that it will not
Committee on Veterans Affairs be possible to discuss an important matter such as the War Veterans Allowance Act.
And so I hope that, even yet, before the debate goes much farther, Liberal members, like the hon. member for Vancouver South and others on that side of the house, who I am sure are just as anxious as we are that something be done on this question, will enter the debate and join with us, as private members on all sides of the house, in making it known to the government that this session must not end without something having been done about the War Veterans Allowance Act.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

Let us be quite frank about this. There is no doubt that people in the country will approve of the stand that the opposition members are taking during the course of this debate. There is no doubt that in time we shall win our point but time can sometimes-
Just before the next election.

speechtext:
-stretch out. The hon. member for Wentworth has just put in a very apt comment; but, Mr. Speaker, this question is serious. We want action, not just approval of the speeches we are making; we want action on this matter at this session of parliament. We believe that it would strengthen our efforts, that it would bring something about for the veterans of this country, if the Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet knew from what was said on the floor of this house that the private members on the Liberal side of the house are just as concerned about this issue as are members on the opposition side of the house.
It has been said by a good many already that it is a bitter disappointment to be told that there are to be no amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session of parliament. As hon. members know, questions on this point have been asked repeatedly during the course of this session. I have asked a number of them myself. The last time that a question on this subject was asked on the orders of the day was on April 30, when the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) put a question to the Prime Minister, after the Prime Minister had listed the remaining items of business for this session of parliament. He asked the Prime Minister whether he had not forgotten to announce an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act. This was the brief reply made by the Prime Minister, as found at page 4276 of Hansard of April 30:
I have stated a complete list of the government's program for the remainder of the session.
That statement seemed to close the door on any possibility of an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session of parliament. But, Mr. Speaker, we have seen doors that were apparently closed, pried open
I Mr. Knowles.]

on previous occasions, and I am joining with other hon. members on this side of the house in asking private members on the government side to join with us in trying to pry this door open so that we might get consideration at this session for those veterans who depend upon the terms of the burnt-out pension or the war veterans allowance.
Of one thing I am sure, despite my lack of confidence in this government. It is that this government would not think of bringing in legislation decreeing that any veteran, or any number of veterans, should be asked to starve. To a great many veterans that is just what it seems like when, with all the rest of the legislation that has been brought in at this session of parliament improving the position of other people, there is nothing to amend the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am sure that this government, in its most callous moments, would not bring in a bill discriminating against our burnt-out pensioners, our burnt-out veterans, particularly those of the first war. It would not bring in a bill saying that their services should be forgotten. But many of those veterans-other hon. members know it as well as I do from the letters they receive from them-feel that that is exactly the kind of treatment that is being accorded them by virtue of failure of the government to do anything about the the War Veterans Allowance Act at this session.
What the government will do regarding legislation is a matter that has to be decided by the cabinet, but surely this simple request that we are making is one that should be met; namely, that this committee's terms of reference should be broadened so that the members of that committee will have the unquestioned right to discuss the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I appeal to the government to consider enlarging the terms of reference. I appeal to Liberal private members in this House of Commons to join with us in making that plea to the government.
