I should like to thank the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) for his courtesy in this matter; I thought it had been brought to his attention. At long last, Mr. Speaker, the resolution having to do with the committee on veterans affairs has been brought before the house. Many veterans throughout Canada and their families will be pleased that the resolution has been acted upon. However, it is something like the very famous old proverb that appears in the Good Book. If I am not correct in this I am sure somebody will call it to my attention. In any event the proverb goes something like this; The mountain laboured and brought forth a mouse. I am quite willing to agree that a mouse, albeit small, is better than no mouse at all.
Hon. members who are to be members of this committee will be very glad to have the committee set up so that we shall be able to get to work on the legislation, such as it is. I should like to agree with the numerous hon. members who have already expressed certain thoughts with respect to this committee, and have also expressed their opinions.
I believe this committee rather than being a special committee ought to be a standing committee of this house. I think the subject of veterans affairs is sufficiently important to justify the appointment of a standing committee. I also agree with other hon. members who have suggested that this committee should have a larger membership. There are a great many members in this house who have served in one or both world wars and who should like to have an opportunity of sitting on this committee. But since the committee is comprised of only 31 members not many of us will have the opportunity to do so.
I was interested in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and his opinion of the manner in which this committee conducted its affairs previously, namely in a non-political manner. Problems concerning war veterans were brought up by committee members themselves and that was an excellent way of running a committee such as this, and I think it would be agreeable if that type of committee were set up again at the next session of this house. I believe all hon. members will agree that veterans affairs is not a subject which should be made a political football.
However, I would like to congratulate the government on the excellent veterans legislation which has been passed in the years since the war. I agree with other hon. members that there may be other countries which
Committee on Veterans Affairs have legislation just as good, but certainly no other country has better legislation. Nevertheless, there is always room for improvement. Since 1945 there has been a great change in conditions in Canada. For example, our population has increased a great deal and the number of new houses has increased considerably in the suburbs of our large cities. Certainly most Canadian cities large or small in Canada have expanded their boundaries and veterans who previously had two or three acre plots in the townships now have their homes in urban areas and carry a much heavier burden of taxation. Moreover, I believe it has been found by experience that while the two and three acre plots were supposed to make people independent in the event of a recession, these plots are much too large to be worked by hand and too small on which to operate machinery. That is just one example of the change which has taken place in Canada. In addition, because of the expansion of our urban areas it is now very difficult for anyone to obtain a plot of a suitable size near his place of employment.
I had hoped that when this committee was set up it would be able to deal with the recommendations set out in the brief presented to the government by the Canadian Legion last fall. I believe the recommendations suggested in that brief were fair and reasonable and not at all out of proportion. These recommendations were carefully thought out and have taken the changing conditions I have outlined into consideration. I am expressing these facts not because I happen to be a member of the Canadian Legion, but because I really believe the recommendations set out in that brief are all worthy of consideration at this time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would just like to comment briefly, without transgressing your ruling today, on certain matters which will be discussed by this committee. The first question to which I would like to refer is the suggested change in the Veterans Land Act. From what we have been able to gather these changes seem very appropriate and will probably be of considerable benefit to veterans and will serve to bring the present legislation into line with conditions existing in this country at the present time.
There is one matter which unfortunately will not, it appears, come before this committee and that is the question of possible amendment to the Pension Act. The minister is no doubt aware that section 13, subclause 1, paragraph (a), and section 13, subclause 1, paragraph (c), which ameliorates the first section I mentioned, cause a great deal of hardship. I just mention that in the hope

Committee on Veterans Affairs that the minister will give it his consideration. I see Mr. Speaker looking at me and I must be rather careful and avoid going into detail.
The last thing I would like to mention in passing is one which has been mentioned by almost every hon. member who has spoken in this debate and that is the matter of veterans allowances. I agree with other hon. members who feel it is a great pity that this committee when it sits will not have an opportunity to consider legislation in this regard. I believe I am quite safe in saying every veterans organization in Canada, and the Canadian Legion in particular, feel this matter of veterans allowance is the prime problem which concerns every veterans organization at the present time. As other hon. members have pointed out, the matter of increasing these allowances and raising the ceiling of permissible income should be brought before this committee. Certainly legislation in this regard is very much needed, and of great importance to veterans generally.
I have heard it said by some veterans that after all in the first year after the election one cannot expect too much, and that possibly some legislation will be introduced at another session, closer possibly to the date of the next election. I am quite sure the government would not like to give veterans the impression that this matter of veterans allowances is being used as a political football. I just mention this because as Shakespeare said: It is not what is truth, but what people believe to be truth. Unfortunately I am afraid a great many veterans will gather that impression.
In conclusion I would just like to reiterate that I hope before the session is concluded that the door may be opened for the committee to examine this question of veterans allowances.

Mr. Speaker, reference was made by two previous speakers this afternoon to directive No. 25, 1953. It will be recalled that during the fall session of this parliament I asked questions of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) regarding this directive which had been issued during the summer when this house was not in session. That directive made changes with respect to casual earnings. At that time casual earnings were defined as that amount of money which might be obtained through odd jobs but not exceeding $2 per day. The minister explained that there was some ambiguity about that definition and very kindly offered to look into the matter. As a result of his investigation and the investigation undertaken by the


chairman of the war veterans allowance board this amendment was introduced. Casual earnings are now defined in a far more generous manner than hitherto. The directive refers to earnings obtained through work in jobs not of a regular nature, and it goes on to say:
Earnings by a recipient and/or his wife resulting from part-time regular employment such as a caretaker for a church or school, a canteen attendant, a crossing guard, self-employment at home on a parttime basis, etc.
Such earnings would be considered as being exempt. Then in another paragraph it goes on to say that earnings by a recipient and his wife resulting from full-time temporary employment of limited duration such as at summer camps, guard duties, collecting tickets at race tracks, replacing a regular employee on holidays, harvesting or other similar activities of relatively short duration would not be considered under the title of that income which would have to be deducted. All those are excellent regulations. I am highly pleased that the minister has been able to authorize that extension. But that extension does not cover the whole field. When this committee is set up I would hope that there will be discussion of these regulations which are in many respects more far-reaching than any of the minor amendments which are being introduced under the different bills to which specific attention has been called in this resolution.
I am not asking for a general discussion necessarily on the War Veterans Allowance Act. I am asking that this memorandum be placed before the committee, partly so that the memorandum may be brought to the attention of the nation. As was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), little publicity has been given to this memorandum. It was issued at the time of the Easter recess and there was little opportunity for anybody to discuss it. If this memorandum is placed before the committee with the amendments to the various other bills which are to be introduced the committee would then have an opportunity to discuss the extent to which this memorandum meets the problem of the older veteran.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to delay the house for long. I am an old soldier, and I am getting older every year. I suppose I am getting more and more cantankerous as the years march on. I am sick to death of pleading with this government for the old soldiers of Canada. I think the time has come when this government needs an urge to do something rather than pleading to do something for the old soldiers. It is my great good fortune-I served in a number of units during

the first war-to have had the opportunity of meeting many of the men who forty years ago this year left Canada to fight for the then king and for this country. Those men are advancing in years. They have given so much in the past that they are finding it utterly impossible, in hundreds of cases, to keep up with the modern trend of life today. They have been looking to this government to do something now to help them meet the critical situation with which they are faced in their declining years.
They have the approach through the Canadian Legion; but only a comparatively small percentage of veterans are in the Canadian Legion; they are not all in it. I wish that every ex-serviceman was a member of the Canadian Legion. Then perhaps the government would pay more attention to what the Legion has to say. They sort of brush them aside because there are only perhaps some 300,000 members in the Legion out of one and a quarter million veterans in Canada. But the Legion speaks for that one and a quarter million veterans, even though they are not all members of the Legion. The Legion has been demanding that something be done for these old soldiers.
It is all very well to ask for extensions of this resolution, but extensions are quite unnecessary. Right there in the wording of this resolution there is ample opportunity for this committee to be given the chance of examining the legislation which is passed. The government itself is issuing a challenge. The government says "and any other legislation which the government may be prepared to place before the committee." All this government has to do is to come forward with amendments to the War Veterans Allowance Act and then the committee can discuss it. It is not for the members of the opposition or for the House of Commons to say whether this problem is going to be discussed in the committee; it is for the government to say that. The government can introduce an amendment. The government knows full well what amendments are required. If there is any doubt at all, then let the committee discuss the matter and make a firm recommendation as to what are the best types of amendments to be made. The amendments suggested by the government can be discussed in the committee and, if necessary, can be modified. But the government is afraid to come forward with any amendment. The government is afraid to place an amendment to the War Veterans Allowance Act before the committee which it itself is recommending to be set up to consider such legislation as it may choose to place before the committee.
Committee on Veterans Affairs
Let the government make the decision. Let the government now choose to bring forward an amendment which will relieve the doubt, uncertainty and suffering with which these old soldiers are now faced. The matter is up to the government. If the government refuses to measure up to its own challenge to place before this committee such legislation as it feels should be placed before it, then that government is guilty of most callous indifference and utter failure to realize the situation which is facing the veterans of Canada today. The government knows what is the situation. The government can bring in the legislation. If it fails to do so, I consider it to be an atrocious affront to the ex-servicemen of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who was extremely anxious to hear what I was going to say, does not seem to be in the house. I have something to say which I am fairly sure he would like to hear. I cannot help recalling to the mind of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes) that I had the honour, a great many years ago- in 1917, I think it was-to occupy the next hospital bed in the field dressing station during the same week that the hon. gentleman won his Victoria Cross. My regard for the hon. gentleman was high then, and it is higher now, even though I think he has developed a louder voice in the subsequent 30 or 35 years.
If my hon. friend and my friends generally in the opposition were sincerely to forget party politics just for a minute I think we would all come to the conclusion that, in spite of all the things that we have done or left undone in this Canada of ours in the past 30 or 35 years, no one could ever accuse this country of being ungrateful to the men who served it in the theatres of war. I say that because there is not an hon. member in this house, there is not an intelligent citizen in the whole Dominion of Canada or, for that matter, in the entire British commonwealth, who does not know that Canada's veterans legislation is the best veterans legislation bar none in the entire world.
I know a little about veterans legislation from both ends, the giving end and the receiving end. I think that I have been in as many veterans hospitals as a patient as probably most hon. members in the house. I must say that I fooled the doctors a bit because after they had washed me up about 30 years ago and had given me only a few months to live I kept out of the hospitals for about 30 years. When I went back

Committee on Veterans Affairs into the hospital last year, probably because of my very bad temper at the change of government in British Columbia, and stayed there for a couple of weeks to recuperate I could not help but be impressed by the fact that in the 30 years since I had been in that hospital the change in the whole veterans administration was really something wonderful. I venture to say that those of us who go next Sunday to see the opening of the wonderful new veterans hospital at Ste. Foy will come to the conclusion that there is not a finer hospital in the country and that the veterans hospitals are on a par with the very finest institutions in this land.
I am frank to confess that I would have preferred it if the government had made the terms of reference of the committee a bit wider. But as the hon. member for Esqui-malt-Saanich suggests, any aggregation of men with good common sense and intelligence can always take terms of reference and interpret them liberally even if they are good, staunch, true blue Tories. I am sorry to say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could not have read the full text of my speech, part of which he quoted this afternoon.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Oh yes, I did.

If he had read in full the speech to which he referred this afternoon he would have seen that while I hoped the government would make the terms of reference wide open, I had had enough experience of the democratic process to know that intelligent people could take any terms of reference and pretty well say anything that requires to be said within those terms.
I tried that this afternoon.

When someone asked our own Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) at the United Nations one time whether such and such a question would come up I remember that he said he was quite sure that, regardless of the agenda, the delegates there would find ways and means to discuss anything that required to be discussed. Therefore I for one have no hesitation whatever in believing that the veterans affairs committee will be an intelligent committee and will find ways and means to discuss anything that falls within its common-sense purview, including the Legion brief or anybody else's brief.
I am sometimes a bit amazed at hon. friends opposite, especially hon. friends immediately opposite me, who always clamour to the high heavens for more welfare legislation. They are for everything so long as it does not have to be paid for. I remember what they said when we introduced the 40-hour week for the post offices.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I realize now how right I was this afternoon when I asked that the rule of relevancy be observed. If there is a wide open discussion there will be rebuttals. I think the hon. member understands that on this resolution, which after all only involves a discussion of the desirability of appointing a committee, something that apparently meets with everybody's approval, his remarks should be relevant to the matter under discussion.

May I say again how
delighted I am-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You see that you do have to stick to the terms of reference.

-with the setting up of the veterans affairs committee. It seems to me that it is one more step in the creation and maintenance of the finest welfare state in the entire world, one other brick in the structure of which will be placed when we get the allowances this week for disabled persons.
Order.

Mr. Speaker, several times during this discussion hon. members have referred to the excellence of the legislation on our statute books concerning the problems of the veterans. No one, I think, is disputing that point and I see no need to continue to emphasize that particular aspect of the topic. Certainly those veterans of world war II, who have benefited from certain phases of the legislation, would agree 100 per cent. When I was discussing the veterans legislation with a certain group of individuals on one occasion they were quite surprised to discover that I had received benefits following the last war. One of them made the observation that perhaps the legislation would have been somewhat different if the government had thought that it was nurturing a viper in its bosom by means of the generous terms accorded to the veterans of world war II.
But I say that to emphasize that particular aspect in our discussion today is really begging the question. As I look at the resolution and try to interpret and understand the terms of reference from the point of view of how far they extend, it seems to me that they will narrow the scope of the veterans affairs committee, and that to do so is a retrograde step in the maintenance of the high level of veterans welfare legislation that we have already achieved in this country. I would suggest that the reason for the high quality of our veterans legislation is the fact, as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard), that the committees which considered this subject

during the war had very broad terms of reference and were widely representative of all groups in the house. I submit that it is because of the wideness of those terms of reference that the legislation we have today was finally realized.
Looking at the resolution, it seems to me that we are moving away from that broader interpretation that has been so successful in the past. We cannot dwell on the past continually, and it is obvious there is some dissatisfaction concerning certain features of veterans legislation. The length of the discussion today would indicate that considerable pressure is building up. As I look at my mail from day to day I find in it letters pertaining to one or two controversial aspects of veterans legislation, and this would tend to suggest that there is some need for a more comprehensive consideration of the legislation than is indicated in the resolution before us this evening. With all the enthusiasm that I can muster I would support the representations of other hon. members that the terms of reference of the committee should be substantially broader than they now are.
Furthermore, I should like to support the suggestion that there should be a standing committee of this house on veterans affairs. I believe this as a result of my experience as a member during the past three years. I am discovering that a good deal of a member's time is spent in the consideration of veterans' welfare problems. I discovered further, as I discussed these matters with the members of the various departments, that there is a great duplication of the information requested concerning problems that arise repeatedly. I am sure that were a committee placed on a standing basis, the administrative officials would welcome the suggestion. It must be a source of great exasperation to them to be repeatedly considering the same problem, going over the same issues, when if we could get together at regular intervals we would find that these problems had assumed a general pattern and helpful solutions could be considered and a broader approach to these recurring difficulties could be realized. I would contend that if we had a standing committee it would have to be larger in terms of numerical membership than the committee indicated by this resolution. In this house there is a growing number of veteran members. I am sure there is not one of them who would not be anxious to have the opportunity to serve on a committee that might be dealing with such an important subject as the welfare of the veterans.
I do not need, Mr. Speaker, to re-emphasize the burning issue that has been repeatedly
Committee on Veterans Affairs discussed today. The problem raised by every hon. member is that of changes in the basic rates and permissible earnings ceiling of war veterans allowances; that seems to be the crux of the controversy here this afternoon. I am sure much time could have been saved and this discussion could have been considerably abbreviated had the resolution, instead of referring obliquely to other legislation relating to veterans affairs, referred specifically to changes in the War Veterans Allowance Act. We could have then moved expeditiously to the establishment of the committee and there, in the close contact that is possible in deliberations of that kind, some successful solution could have been realized in regard to representations being made by all veterans groups concerning changes in the war veterans allowances.
I refer particularly, of course, to the work of the Canadian Legion in this respect. Again the Canadian Legion deserves much of the credit for the high quality of our veterans legislation. It is my hope that during the committee sessions we shall have an opportunity to hear from responsible representatives of the Canadian Legion. It would still be possible, as a result of those representations, to come to grips with the urgent need of doing something about the upward revision of the terms of the war veterans allowance.

I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) is now well aware of the fact that the subject of veterans legislation is of serious importance to the members of this house. It is not a subject that can be introduced and disposed of in a few minutes. It is a subject that is treated with great seriousness by the members of this house and the people across the country.
I hope the minister realizes that there is great disappointment in his action in bringing this resolution to the attention of the House of Commons. It has been on the order paper for three months and we expected something different when the minister made his announcement on February 11 that the committee would be appointed. We thought then he was going to meet the demands that have been made from time to time in this house for a committee to consider all the problems affecting veterans. Instead of that we have a bit of camouflage in this resolution, and we have a so-called committee on veterans affairs that is really a special committee to deal with several bills affecting veterans.
According to the terms of reference, it is not intended that the committee shall look
4584	HOUSE OF
Committee on Veterans Affairs further afield and look into some of the pressing problems affecting veterans. The terms of reference are restricted. From time to time a request has been made for a standing committee on veterans affairs, and with good reason. People in the house today, and on other occasions, have mentioned the excellence of the veterans legislation in Canada. I do not question that at all. I have not had the opportunity of making comparisons that others have made. It may be excellent, but that does not say it could not be improved. The fact our veterans legislation is better than that of some other country is no reason for resting on our laurels and not making the necessary improvements.
It has never been proved.

The hem. member for Royal suggests it has not been proved. I believe there are serious weaknesses in the veterans legislation. Perhaps those weaknesses are not in the charter but in the field of administration. This places the matter right before the minister. It is for that reason that a standing committee on veterans affairs, convened early in the session and given the opportunity to investigate the whole field of veterans legislation, would be able to find out the reason for the weaknesses that are only too apparent in the management of veterans affairs in Canada.
Let us just consider the need for investigating veterans problems. They are continuing problems. There are veterans of the first world war, ageing but many of them still alive. There are the veterans of the second world war and the veterans of Korea. Then for the first time in our history we have a large active army. We have no reason for too much confidence that there may not be other conflicts in which our young men may be engaged. We are faced, therefore, with veterans problems for many years in the future. So it is a matter of necessity that we carefully examine our veterans legislation and improve it from time to time to meet changed conditions. That is what has been asked for in this house. That is why we have objected to the terms of reference of this committee, which are so narrow. That is why we draw attention to the fact that one of the most pressing problems in Canada, that of war veterans allowances, is not being dealt with at this session,
Just consider the magnitude of the task with regard to veterans problems. Pensioners alone number 115,000, and each year applications are received for pensions, or for the reconsideration of pensions. An enormous amount of work is being carried out by departmental officials, by representatives of the Legion and by other organized veterans


bodies across this country. I doubt if there is a member of the House of Commons who is not faced with some pressing veterans problems every month.
The magnitude of the task encourages us to press for an investigation of the veterans charter itself, and the administration thereunder. For example, last year there were 3,820 new awards for pensions. Of that number we are told 311 were for first-war applicants. Yet 35 years have elapsed since the conclusion of that war. Do we never solve the problems of the men of the first war, or do they have to die before the department is released from its bond?
One would have thought that by now, after all these years, there would be very few cases concerning veterans of the first war. What is the reason for the recurrence of these problems? Why are there so many of them? The report of the minister's department indicates that each year there are successive appeals, or applications for pensions by men of the first world war. These are followed by second hearings, by third hearings, by appeals and so on. The applications alone numbered more than four thousand in the last year. Of those a thousand were concerned with first war problems.
So I suggest that this is a matter of considerable magnitude. When we turn to the war veterans allowances branch we find again that the numbers are large. In the last 23 years 100,000 have been considered for war veterans allowances. The present figure is just under 40,000. Obviously soldiers of the first world war are dying off, so that from the financial point of view the problem is not as serious for the government. But the problem is still there. And with the men of the first world war now in their sixties and seventies-and I believe the average age is somewhere in the sixties- these are the ones requiring attention; and that attention should be given to them.
After 35 years surely we can meet this final obligation to men of the first world war, and settle this problem. But it is a problem to which the minister will not face up; because we know this question has been before the House of Commons year after year. We have been led to believe or have inferred that something would be done about it; yet once again nothing is being done. Hence the protest on this occasion concerning the narrow terms of reference in the resolution before us, and the attitude of the government toward this one problem affecting the veterans which, in the last two or three years, has become a problem of major importance. The number of men applying for war veterans allowances is increasing from year to year; but the number who

remain on the roll does not get very much larger because the older ones are dying off.
This is the situation we are asking to have settled; and it can still be done. The minister can alter his terms of reference to suit the events of the moment. Other members of the House of Commons can join in the demand that the terms of reference be widened. It could still be done this year, so that these older men who have served their country so faithfully may receive their just reward. And let us not forget that that was the purpose and the intent of the veterans legislation. In the book published by the minister of veterans affairs who held office in 1947, the late Right Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, at the back there is a chapter headed "The History of Veterans Legislation in Canada", and at page 285 I read these words:
"The Veterans Charter", states the Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie, K.C., M.P., Minister of Veterans Affairs, "grew in spirit, substance and final form, out of the hearts and minds of a united people dedicating themselves and the lives of their sons and daughters to victory. Its basic provisions were the result of a desire to deal in a just manner with all who served."
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we are to deal in a just manner with all who served we must approach the problem and get to grips with it. We have to have a committee that will deal broadly with all the problems of the veterans, a committee that will solve the problems of the older veterans and that of veterans allowances, a committee that will examine the whole system of the administration of this department, of the administration of the pension commission and of the veterans bureau, a committee that will determine what if anything is the matter-and I think there is something the matter-with veterans legislation itself, or the administration thereof.
Why are there so many cases each year? Why are there so many first hearings, second hearings, third hearings, fourth hearings and further hearings-and sometimes I notice that if you reach the fifth hearing you get results. But you do not get results on the first, second, third or fourth. Surely there is something wrong with our legislation or the interpretation thereof when it results in this type of extensive review of cases. Why is a case, which on its fifth hearing is settled favourably to the applicant, not settled at the first or second hearing? What is wrong? I cannot think new evidence is being brought forward, because everything is documented from the day a man enters the army until the day of his discharge. In some instances there may be new evidence; but I think the defect lies somewhere in the act, something that should be written into it, some interpretation of it that has to be revised. I find the pension commission and the veterans bureau have to
Committee on Veterans Affairs deal with the problem of interpretation and put forth arguments as to how this or that phrase in the act may be interpreted. Are we informed of this body of interpretive law that is being built up with regard to the veterans charter? We would be if we had a standing committee on veterans affairs. These cases would be brought to our attention.
A standing committee on veterans affairs, looking closely into this matter, would ask for an interpretation of sections of acts that are not clear. Perhaps they would be able then to suggest amendments to the minister so the act could be clarified. By that means we would come not only to the assistance of the veterans themselves but also to the assistance of those people who are doing the hard work in the veterans bureau and in the pension commission. I am sure they would like to have some guidance from parliament in the solution of some of these borderline cases and some of the difficult problems that face them. I am not at all of the opinion that they are being too strict with veterans applications, or anything of that nature. They are bound by the instructions that they have to follow, and it is up to parliament itself to make those instructions broad enough and clear enough so that we do justice to those who served.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, that is the reason for this protest of mine against the action of the minister on this occasion. On February 11 he promised us a committee on veterans affairs, and he ended up three months later with a special committee to discuss two or three acts, with small amendments thereto, and avoided the main issue of all that has been before us during the last two years, namely, the problem of war veterans allowances, and he certainly avoided a broad investigation of the veterans charter itself and the administration thereof.

I have been in this house a short while, but time seems to have passed very quickly. I have never been disappointed with the ministers of veterans affairs and the legislation they have brought in. The opposition are doing a pretty good job at this time in trying to show the weaknesses of this resolution, but I admit that they have a stiff job to prove it. I should like to ask the minister a question, which he can answer when he speaks to close the debate. In the resolution I find these words:
and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee.
My question to the minister is this: Can any member of the committee not stand up and ask that a veteran of the first war have his old age pension without a means test at
4586	HOUSE OF
Committee on Veterans Affairs 60? Can he ask that question and any other questions? This resolution is just as wide as the English language can make it, and the committee can ask any question. What is the business of the committee? What are they appointed for? Let them do their job and ask these questions of the minister, and I think we shall have legislation that the veterans of this country will be proud of.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the veterans and veterans organizations welcomed the government's notice some time ago that a special committee was to be set up to consider veterans legislation. Certain measures have been referred to that committee for consideration, such as the War Service Grants Act and a bill respecting benefits for the members of the Canadian forces, and perhaps one or two others. I know that the veterans and those associations are grateful for the legislation that has been brought in over the years, and without question it has brought many advantages to them. However, even if we admit that, we must also recognize the fact that they are far from satisfied with the present legislation on the statute books.
I discussed the matter with a number of the leaders of the Legion in various sections of my riding. They mentioned several things that they would like to see done, and other matters they would like to have considered. They find it difficult to understand why the government is not willing to accede to the request for a standing committee on veterans affairs, since we realize that these problems are with us and apparently will be with us for some considerable time.
It is the general feeling that if such a committee were set up it could deal with these problems as they arise. I am sure that veterans are going to be far from satisfied with the terms of reference of this particular committee. I may not fully understand the terms of reference, but it seems to me that some hon. members who have spoken this afternoon have said that the terms of reference are wide enough, or that we can get around them or under them or over them. That does not seem to fit in with my conception of terms of reference, and certainly this afternoon we were kept pretty close to the line. We were not permitted to discuss too much that went beyond the actual matters that were brought to us in this resolution, and it would seem to me that in the committee the same thing will happen. We will not be given too much latitude as far as discussing the other problems is concerned.
In my conversation with leaders of the Legion group they have mentioned several


problems, and I am sure that the matters referred to the committee are not the major problems as far as the war veterans are concerned. They may be the concern of some, and I have no doubt they are, but I believe that once again the government is failing to face the problems and measure up to the expectations of the veterans and the veterans organizations.
Some major problems have been referred to today, and perhaps I could do no better than just say that I agree with the statement that certain things of paramount importance have been omitted. For instance, there is the matter of war veterans allowances, which we feel are far too low to meet the needs of men at this particular time, and at the present cost of living. I spoke to one particular leader who was on his way back to the coast. I am not sure of his name, but I think it was Williams. He told me that one of the things that helped the war veterans considerably was the fact that they could buy tinned meat so cheaply at the coast. He said it was a Godsend to them because they could not afford to buy fresh meat; they could not afford to buy the better type of meat and therefore they were living on the very cheapest that they could obtain. I feel that this is one of the problems of major concern, but apparently the government is not planning to give any consideration to the matter at all. I fear they will see to it that these terms of reference are tight enough to restrain anyone from dealing with it very effectively.
Another problem has been mentioned to me, namely, the problem of permissive ceiling, which again reminds us that at the present cost of living these ceilings are far too low. I would like to call attention if I could to some articles, but I suppose the Speaker would rule me out of order and therefore I shall refrain from referring to them. But I should like to ask by what process of reasoning is this ceiling maintained? Are we afraid that the veterans are going to get too rich? Just why do we maintain that ceiling on permissive incomes? I have heard it suggested that it is done to keep them more or less in line with the old age pensions and so on. Well, the same thing obtains there. I cannot see why it should be retained on the old age pension basis. I feel the veterans should be encouraged, rather than discouraged, to supplement their allowances to a point where they can maintain an adequate and a decent standard of living.
Another matter has been brought to my attention, and I believe that this could be considered and will be considered by the

committee, since it falls within the terms of reference. I refer to the changes in the regulations relating to earned income. I have been given to understand that that regulation stipulates that 50 per cent of the gross revenue derived from agricultural operations shall be considered as income for the purpose of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Now, Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why we should consider that regulation just and proper. However, I believe the Department of Veterans Affairs is giving consideration to this matter and I trust their ruling will be fair and equitable as far as the veteran engaged in agricultural activities is concerned.
There are other matters to which I would like to refer, Mr. Speaker, but I do not wish to presume on the time of the house. Nevertheless, I feel there are three reasons why at this particular time we ought to give serious consideration to the plight of the war veteran. I believe gratitude demands that something further be done for these men who have hazarded their lives in the defence of the things we hold dear. They were willing to sacrifice everything they had. They sacrificed in their own lives everything that was dear unto them, and they were willing and to all intents and purposes did lay down their lives, just as did others, in the defence of the sacred things we enjoy. Therefore, I would suggest that we take a look at this situation again and reconsider some of the major problems. We request that the minister give consideration to these problems at this particular time and deal with them more effectively than has been the case in the past.
Again, I believe it is our responsibility to see to it that these men have sufficient to maintain them in a decent standard of living. I say we are grateful to them, and our gratitude demands that we do something to discharge the responsibility which devolves upon this government at the present time in regard to these war veterans.
Finally, I believe there is one other consideration, namely that consistency demands that the government do something further for these men at this time. A short time ago legislation was introduced in this house which was bitterly opposed by some and supported by others. 1 happen to be a representative of a group which supported that particular legislation. All hon. members I believe will realize that I am referring to the recent increase in indemnity for members of parliament. The government introduced that legislation and it was approved and we are all much better off for it. I supported that legislation and the group to which I belong supported it, but I feel that because of that there
Committee on Veterans Affairs is an added responsibility upon this government to deal with problems affecting our war veterans. I cannot speak for other hon. members but I can say that I received some letters which were far from complimentary, and I was charged with feathering my own nest, and being interested only in myself. But I assured these individual war veterans, old age pensioners and others that I was just as anxious and more anxious to do something for them than I was in doing something for myself.
In view of that I would urge the government that they shoulder this added responsibility which devolves upon them, and do something now for those who are less fortunate, those who have given so much and who are suffering so much in so many ways. I would urge the government to take note of the privations being suffered by these men and request the minister to give further consideration to this matter and bring in legislation at an early date which will deal effectively with this situation.
In closing I should like to read a letter addressed to the editor of the Vancouver Sun and signed "Old Vet". The letter reads as follows:
We who are about to die salute you. I speak for the burnt-out pensioners between 70 and 90, first war men.
We appeal to you and your intelligent readers against the action of the D.V.A. in reducing war veterans' allowances. We find as we go on the old age pension they cut our W.V. allowance as veterans to $20, making a maximum of $60 a month.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon. member
started out with very good intentions, but I think in reading a letter into the record without divulging the source he is getting away from the rules. The hon. member is aware that he should not read documents, telegrams, or letters unless he is prepared to give the source. It may be that before I resumed the chair he had given the name of the person whose letter he is now reading.

I am very sorry, Mr. Speaker, that you have found it necessary to call me to order, but this letter was written to the editor of the Vancouver Sun and was signed "Old Vet". However, it goes on to say that because of the mere pittance upon which these men were forced to exist they could not pay for necessities, and because of lack of suitable clothing could not attend "the means of grace" on Sunday, and the letter urges that hon. members as they take their place in Ottawa support these people in their request.

Mr. Speaker, like most of the veterans across this country I was very pleased when I saw this resolution

Committee on Veterans Affairs appear on the order paper three months ago tomorrow. There was one reservation though with regard to it, and that was the fact that it did not specifically mention any legislation with the exception of the two bills which are to be referred to this committee when it is set up.
Nevertheless, there is a line in the resolution which reads:
. . . and such other legislation relating to veterans affairs as may be referred from time to time to the said committee . . .
This held out a hope in the minds of most veterans, especially those who are veterans of world war I, that the government during this session intended to present amendments to other veterans legislation which could be dealt with by this same committee.
As time went on it became more and more evident that in effect the terms of reference were not to be widened and, in addition, that this line as it relates to other legislation will probably be meaningless. Added to that there was the disappointment that this committee was merely to be a special committee for the session rather than a standing committee. I believe it is important that we should have a standing committee. I believe it is important that we should have a standing committee of this house on veterans affairs. After all, we in this country have perhaps a million and a half veterans from four different wars, veterans who served in different theatres of war in different circumstances, and it is very difficult to draft legislation which can be interpreted in a manner which will be fair to all. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, at this time I want to express my disappointment that this committee has not wider terms of reference which would allow it to examine the additional legislation which it was hoped this government would bring before parliament during this session.
It is not my intention to transgress the rules of the house by discussing in detail the legislation I believe should have been brought down at this session and referred to this committee. Therefore I conclude my remarks by saying that I hope to deal with some of these subjects when the estimates of the minister's department are before the committee of the whole house. The matter can be discussed more fully at that time, if in the meantime the minister does not relent and decide to bring in some additional amendments to some of the veterans legislation now on the statute books. The whole veteran body of this country hoped that such amendments would be brought down.

Mr. Speaker, a number of hon. members have mentioned the melancholy fact that it is 35 years since the first world war ended. I say


"melancholy" because for those of us who are veterans of that war it brings to mind the unfortunate fact that we are now becoming old men.
Today at noon I took a walk on a pathway around these buildings. If the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) were here I would give him a piece of my mind about the condition of those paths. It is almost 40 years-39 to be precise-since I took that walk previously when I was in Ottawa waiting to go overseas in the first war. During these last few days, Mr. Speaker, knowing that this particular resolution was coming before us, I have been thinking of just what one should say in order to try to bring home to the members of the House of Commons of Canada the obligation they owe to the men who now survive from the first world war. Not many of us are left. Some of us, more by good luck than good guidance, are in a position in which we do not have to come to the people of Canada to enable us to live decently; but a great many are forced to come to the people of Canada.
I am going to suggest this to you, Mr. Speaker. A country such as Canada is today, in 1954-which is a far different country from the Canada of 1914-has no excuse whatever for niggardliness, caution or parsimony in the method of its treatment of the survivors of the first world war. I am not suggesting that those who went away from Canada in that distant summer of 1914 or 1915 were all heroes. We were not; we were ordinary, common human beings. However, I suggest this, Mr. Speaker. A vast number of those who came back from that war came back crippled physically or mentally or perhaps psychologically, and they were unable to find their place in a world to which they were not accustomed. Many of them perhaps, like myself, went into the army as mere boys, straight from school. We were not trained to find our way in a world of peace; we were trained to survive in a world of war. We were trained, in fact, to die and not to live. However, some of us survived and we had to learn how to live. It has not always been easy to do this.
I am going to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the record of Canada with regard to the veterans of the first world war is not so noble and so high-minded as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) would have us believe it to be. I realize, of course, that the hon. member for Vancouver South is the self-appointed leader of the Greek chorus of paeans of praise for everything the Liberal government does. Nevertheless, I am going to suggest that the Liberal government and its predecessors have not always

been models of generosity. I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that on occasion they have been deplorably mean and small-minded.
It has been stated here that the government has done a very good job with regard to veterans affairs. Undoubtedly it has done a fairly good job. Like the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), I am not in a position to measure their accomplishments against those of other governments. However, I doubt whether Canada will stand so very far ahead of other nations of the world in that regard. I also greatly doubt whether our record is commensurate with our ability to carry out our obligations to those whom we asked to risk their lives in the service of this country. I am going to ask the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and this government if they really think that even the most extravagant demands from those who served Canada-those who, incidentally, not many years ago were practically promised the moon in exchange for their patriotic services-are going to break Canada? Do we really have to watch our pennies so carefully? As to every man who comes to us and says "You owe me a pension because I gave service in the armed forces of this country", do we have to be quite sure that he is not going to cheat us? Does it matter, Mr. Speaker? I for one would rather have the government and the people of Canada cheated by a hundred charlatans than to have one deserving case treated in a niggardly manner.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I would ask this government to take a second thought and to give us a wide-open committee, one which will have power to consider all the problems of the veterans of the first war, of the second world war and of the Korean war and to advance the most generous proposals. I suggest to you that the people of Canada will support their government in the most generous considerations they may make with regard to the situation of those whom we have called upon from time to time to risk their lives in the defence of this country and of the values for which this country stands. We cannot take one position when we are in danger and another When that danger has been removed.
I have never been able to forget an incident when a number of young men who had been wandering, homeless and destitute, across this country came to see me in Victoria to say good-bye before they left on the adventure of the second world war to defend a democracy that had given them destitution and a country which had had no use for their services. I cannot forget that those young men, nevertheless, went to deal
Committee on Veterans Affairs for us with the appalling danger of the nazi menace to human civilization. I say this to you, Mr. Speaker. No matter what the circumstances of what any of those individuals may be or no matter how weak a character such a man may be in civilian life, you and I owe him a duty. We owe our self-respect a duty. I trust that this government, which is spending money with such a lavish hand on some extremely dubious enterprises for which I have yet to hear any reasonable justification, will on this occasion decide to listen perhaps to the voice of the opposition and to alter the terms of reference of this committee.
It may be, as the hon. member for Vancouver South says, that on this occasion, unlike all other occasions, this committee will be able to disregard its terms of reference. It may be that this Liberal government is different from other Liberal governments which I have faced in earlier times. But unless it is different I know very well that the committee will be held down rigidly to the very letter of the terms of reference, that no member will be allowed to stray one inch beyond. I am going to suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that this government and this parliament will not be discharging their responsibility to the people of Canada and to the veterans of the Canadian armed forces unless they insist that the terms of reference of the committee be widened and that the committee be constituted as a standing committee of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, to the best of my recollection I have never spoken in this debate before. When I first had the honour of being a member of this house I felt that the affairs of veterans were in good hands. I think they were in good hands all through the house. The late Ian Mackenzie, who had much to do with them in those days, was a man of the widest sympathy who really made the cause of the veterans his own. And all through the house there were others. But I feel that tonight I should like to add a very few words. I hardly know why except I think as time goes on and as those of us with whom life has dealt more kindly meet the comrades of those years we realize more than we did then that those who were most useful in war are often not the most useful in peace. We remember them as they were then, how brave, how gay, how humorous, and we often meet them now and realize that they have not fared very well in life. I suppose that as we and they grow older that feeling grows.
There is only one point I want to make. It seems to me that there is a very small

Committee on Veterans Affairs difference dividing us at the present time and that it could easily be resolved. What is being asked of the government is that they extend the terms of reference. I am not going into the merits of that. It has been adequately dealt with, I merely want to stress the fact that I think the difference is not a very great one. On the other hand, I think that for the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Philpott) to suggest that a committee that is appointed to deal with A, B and C could rollick along and deal with D, E and F is not very sensible. That does not seem to be a serious contribution to the debate because even a person who knows as little of the rules as I do knows that we would not get very far if we did that kind of thing.
On the other hand, I feel that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) was absolutely correct when he said this afternoon there were many in all parts of the house who would like to see this matter discussed in broad fashion. I think many people agreed with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he said that this was not a committee to deal with veterans affairs but a committee to deal with the War Service Grants Act and the bill respecting benefits for members of the Canadian forces. I think that was true. I repeat that I think the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra was representing the feelings of the house when he said that there would be a widespread disposition to have the matter discussed. And why not? Has the government not got ample safeguards? They will of course have a majority on the committee itself which I take it will not be wholly deaf to their wishes. They will then have their majority in the house which also is not deaf to their wishes. Why in those circumstances should it not be possible to have this matter discussed freely, frankly and in broad terms?
No one is asking-at least, I am not and I do not think anyone else is-for a committee committed in advance. All that we are asking is that this matter, which I believe is dear to the hearts of every member of the house, should be discussed in wide-open fashion. I find myself somewhat embarrassed perhaps in suggesting what may involve extra expenditure, but I would just conclude these remarks with these words:	If we find what the
amount is, if we find that we think something more should be done, then whatever else we do, whatever other economies we make, we should not make economies at the expense of what is right and just to these men.

Mr. Speaker, in two terrible wars the noble youth of Canada have risen, marched, and stood, sufficient in their generation. But for their strivings, their sacrifices, and those of the hundreds of thousands of others from the vast expanses of the British Empire and commonwealth, we should not be sitting in this house today, or dwelling in the matchless land of Canada. The best we can possibly do is too little to compensate them for the measureless losses numbers of them have sustained. Considering the rich and varied wealth of production of which this nation is capable, and of which this nation has proved herself capable by actual achievement, the treatment that Canada has accorded to far too many of her veterans, right from the beginning, has been meagre, if not downright niggardly.
The requests of our veterans have in the main been moderate indeed. Their present requests are moderate. Take, for instance, the request that the war veterans allowance be raised to $60 a month for a single man. Who can possibly call that extreme? Take the request that the allowance be raised to $120 a month for a married man. I should like to see any member of the cabinet of Canada get out and try to live with a wife on $120 a a month. Far too many of our people have been raised with silver spoons in their mouths. They just do not know what it means to be up against rough going.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: A good many of us have.

Take another instance, the request that the ceiling on permissive income be raised to $1,000 for a single man. To deny any man in Canada the privilege of earning as much as that is to subject him almost to slavery. The same is true of the request that permissive income be raised to $2,000 for a married man.
For years now I have been contemplating the treatment we have been giving our returned men. During recent sessions I have not voiced my disapproval to any great extent, although in former years I did. But it has always been a conundrum to me what could be the basic reason for the way we treat our men. Is it, Mr. Speaker, that some hidden hand behind the government of Canada is deliberately causing the Canadian government to mistreat our returned men so as to discourage the youth of the rising generation from joining the forces, thereby weakening the fighting potential of this nation? Could that be the reason? Certainly it is not financial. It is not the fact that we cannot produce enough. There must be some sinister, hidden reason.

Mr. Speaker, when you contrast the loyalty, the fervent devotion, faith and confidence with which the boys of my generation arose and flocked to the colours, then marched off to die, contrast it with the cynicism that prevailed far too commonly amongst the boys who entered world war II, and to a worse extent than that, prevails in the hearts of too many men today, you wonder how it can have come to be. They are of the selfsame blood, of the same race, bear the same names; they have over them the same flag. What has caused the appalling deterioration?
I do not propose to enter into that tonight. I suggest that if we desired to destroy this nation-I sometimes wonder if the members of the government do not want to do that- if we desired to destroy the British commonwealth, drag down the union jack and trample it in the mud or see some foreign people do that, I do not see how we could possibly guide ourselves more unerringly to that goal than we are doing in the way we are dealing with many of our returned men.
I am not saying that we are not giving many of the boys fine opportunities. I have been delighted with the consideration, the tenderness and the earnestness that I have seen manifested by the men in our departments when dealing with veterans. The difficulty is that the damage is done before these people ever get a chance. The damage is done when the bills are passed, the rules are drafted and the directives are issued.

speechtext:
Order. Could the hon.
member make these remarks when the estimates for the Department of Veterans Affairs are before the house? I have asked hon. members not to deal with veterans affairs generally, and I think they have been trying to do that. I know the hon. member wishes to conform with the rules, just as the others have. I do not want to be less generous in my attitude towards him than I was towards the others, but it seems to me we are getting rather far afield in the resolution stage of setting up a committee to study two bills and other legislation that may be brought before the house.
I do not want to have to intervene too often. I know it is always disagreeable, both to the hon. member who is being interrupted and to myself. I would ask the hon. member to confine his remarks to the subject matter of the resolution.

I thank you most earnestly for your most gracious way of pointing out to me that I have been deviating. May I assure you that I shall discontinue, having
Committee on Veterans Affairs left those questions for every hon. member in this house and every person in the country to answer.

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
In rising to close the debate on this resolution to set up the committee on veterans affairs I feel that my remarks should be brief. I feel that first because I believe there are very few matters pertaining to the subject that have not been dealt with already by the speakers who have taken part in the debate. Secondly, any statement I might make in answer to the charges that have been levelled at the minister and the government on this particular resolution is limited by the ruling that you rendered this afternoon, Mr. Speaker.
There are a few remarks, though, that I should like to make dealing with some of the points raised by hon. members. During the course of the debate everyone expressed particular pleasure, in a rather sarcastic manner, over the fact that this resolution had, at long last, been called. I do not feel I have to make any apologies in that respect, Mr. Speaker. I have explained to some hon. members privately when they asked me the reason for the delay in calling this resolution. Some of the legislation the government wants to introduce, and which will be introduced in a few days I hope, is still in the drafting process. This is something of a technical character. The amendments to the Veterans Land Act are rather lengthy, and in the face of a considerable amount of work the staff whose special work it is to draft this legislation has not been able to produce the bill within the time I had hoped.
I have felt, and I think rightly, it would be preferable to wait until I was sure I would not have to bring the committee together to study some of the legislation, and then postpone further hearings for a matter of weeks. One of the reasons for this is that in the past it has been the practice of national veterans organizations to come before the committee to express their views on matters which interest them, regardless of the terms of reference.
These gentlemen come from all parts of Canada and so I felt it would be more appropriate to wait until I could bring all the legislation before the committee and have these groups make only one trip to Ottawa to make their representations to the committee. I feel I have no apologies to make for this.
Many members have expressed the view that the government should accede to the
4592	HOUSE OF
Committee on Veterans Affairs demand made in the last few years that the veterans affairs committee should be a standing committee, that is a committee under standing order 63. I believe that the whole matter of parliamentary committees is one of the subjects being studied by the rules committee which has been set up to look into the rules, standing orders and procedure of the house. I believe this committee is inquiring into the whole structure of parliamentary committees and reporting upon them. I have no doubt if that committee, of which many of those who spoke are members, does make such a recommendation the government will certainly give it most serious consideration.
I might point out, however, that I believe some hon. members, in making that suggestion, have in mind an objective that might not be accomplished simply by setting up a standing committee on veterans affairs. I am not an expert on parliamentary procedure, but I have no doubt that if my assumptions are wrong hon. members opposite, and particularly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), will set me straight.
My understanding is that a parliamentary committee, whether it is a special select committee or a standing committee, can deal only with matters that are referred to it by the House of Commons. And the fact that our standing orders might be amended so that the veterans affairs committee would be made a standing committee would not necessarily mean that this committee each year, on its own authority, could investigate and inquire into every phase of veterans legislation,	and report	upon it to
the House of Commons. I think this should be remembered. However, as I say, 1 have no particular views to propose on the matter. I have no doubt that this and other committees are subjects which will be looked into and reported upon by the rules committee of the house.
Hon. members have complained considerably of the fact that the terms of reference of this committee are very restricted. I believe it was the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green)-and if I am wrong I should be pleased to be corrected- who said that the only bills mentioned were minor amendments. He intimated that the Veterans Benefit Act and the War Service Grants Act amendments were minor.
On a point of order; I did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, then; I was not sure. Then, I think it was the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) who said that.
No, I did not say they were minor amendments. I said they were not as important as the minister tried to make out they were, as compared with other amendments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Try again.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I think the record will show that the hon. member used the word "minor". However, I am willing to accept his correction. I would like to point out that these bills, as I said earlier, are the bills which put into statutory form the various legislation applicable to Korean veterans. I recall very well that when the Veterans Benefit Act was introduced in the house by myself on the first occasion hon. members asked why these provisions were not put into statutory form, and why the legislation was going to be carried out by orders in council. I explained at the time that it was necessary and that it would make it more flexible. I pointed out that we did not know yet just what the circumstances of the service would be. And when each year I introduced a bill to continue the powers of the governor in council under the Veterans Benefit Act, to implement those provisions, I was told that it should be put in statutory form. Now hon. members say that it is minor legislation which really did not require the creation of a veterans affairs committee.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is other legislation of equal importance. On the order paper there stands a bill to amend the Pension Act. The resolution has already been passed, and second reading of the bill was called for today and would have been proceeded with if this debate had not continued all day.
I might point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill), who in his criticism of the resolution mentioned various aspects of the Pension Act and regretted what he considered a restriction in the terms of reference of the committee, that there is a bill concerning the Pension Act that will be referred to that committee. He will be able there to inquire into each one of the points he mentioned when he was making his criticism of the terms of reference.
Then, as I pointed out earlier there is legislation concerning the Veterans Land Act. I hope to be able to introduce it in a few days. I am awaiting final draft from the legal experts.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that in the past the veterans in this country have benefited by the joint work of all members of the House of Commons who have served on veterans affairs committees. They have done good work over those many years under terms of reference that have varied greatly. When

hon. members say that only in the last tew years have the terms of reference for veterans affairs committees been restricted, I would suggest that they go right back to the first committees which were set up after the first world war and find out for themselves what the terms of reference were. If they will read the reports of those committees they will find that most of the subjects which this committee will be able to discuss, when it is appointed and nominated, were not and could not be discussed under those terms of reference.
I hope we will be able-and I see no reason why we should not-to continue to work in the veterans affairs committee as we have done in the past, in that same spirit of co-operation, and with the same aim as previous committees have had, namely the general welfare of all the veterans in this country.

One question; has the
minister nothing to say about the omission of the War Veterans Allowance Act in this resolution?
